speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: FURTHER CANADIAN MILITARY COMMITMENTS
speechtext: When we form part of an alliance, Mr. Speaker, we do so in good faith. speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Can the minister say what steps are being taken by the government with respect to the recent storm damage in Newfoundland?

subtopic: STORM DAMAGE IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
The attitude of the federal government towards such catastrophes in provinces has
322

Inquiries of the Ministry been stated by the Prime Minister on several occasions, and it has been that property rights are primarily a matter for the provinces. It is only in cases where the losses in such catastrophes are beyond the financial ability of the province to handle that the federal government does assist. Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to table an order in council passed today having to do with the remission of interest on instalments paid pursuant to the provisions of section 47 of the Income Tax Act, and relating to the fiscal periods ending prior to May 1, 1953, by corporations which were liable to tax on net income under the corporation tax act, 1939 (Ontario), where these are insufficient as a result of the deduction of an amount or amounts calculated under the provisions of section 37 of the Income Tax Act.
In that connection I wish to make the following statement as it is of interest to business corporations in Ontario.
As a result of the tax agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Ontario, signed on October 29, 1952, being made retroactive to January 1, 1952, corporate taxpayers carrying on business in Ontario may have underpaid instalments of federal income tax. In view of the inequity of charging interest on the deficient instalments of federal income tax caused in this way, the provisions of the Financial Administration Act have been invoked to remit such interest, in so far as the under-remittance of instalments relates to the 5 per cent tax formerly deductible under section 37 of the Income Tax Act, and for the period up to the 31st December, 1952. In the result, corporations formerly paying corporation tax in Ontario will not be charged interest on the deficiency in their instalment payments of federal income tax to the extent that these instalments have been reduced in anticipation of the obligation to pay Ontario corporation tax, provided that their position is corrected before December 31 of this year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, December 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. L. Deslieres for an address to his Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I propose to deal with the trade policies of the government as related also to the trade policies of the official opposition. In western Canada we are probably more aware or more conscious of the importance of our export trade than are any other parts of Canada. Through experience we have learned that our prosperity, our standard of living, is directly tied up to the markets that can be found for our products outside of Canada. Consequently, anything that is said or done about this vital question of export trade is of great interest, and indeed of great concern, to all of us in western Canada. As a matter of fact, this question of export trade affects not only that part of Canada but all parts of Canada since history and the record prove that when our export trade was high, the country went through a period of prosperity.
Naturally, we were interested when the leader of the official opposition announced that he was going abroad, particularly to the United Kingdom and to Europe, on a factfinding tour in order to find a solution for some of the problems and then to offer suggestions upon his return. From press releases we found that when he returned to Canada he was rather reticent in his remarks and in the announcement of his policy. As a matter of fact, from the press releases it would appear that he more or less took the attitude: "Elect me first, and then I will tell you what my policy is." However, shortly after his return he was out on a tour of the western provinces, and then he toured some of the eastern provinces. Of course, since the house has been sitting we have heard gradually the announcement of that policy and the echo in the official opposition in the house. We find now that their policy is simply to revive, or to retransplant into Canada, the old Tory school of England who advocate the creation of British commonwealth and empire blocs, higher tariff walls and self-sufficiency, to some degree at least, regardless of the cost to the country.
When the Leader of the Opposition was in my province, he was naturally asked many questions on the policy itself. It is obvious that he tried, to the best of his ability, to
hide the true identity of the policy, through various means of using fancy words and press denials. However, this policy is so well known that I am sure nobody can forget it, particularly in western Canada, and it was soon recognized. I am not surprised at the Social Credit party swallowing this from the official opposition, because, as we know, most of the Social Crediters are Tories in background.	;

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is an absolute falsehood.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They are just ordinary Tories, with a variety of bibles thrown in. I was more surprised, however, to see the socialists fall for the same policy as well. The only explanation I can find is that they see a possibility of their dream coming .true, because they have always dreamed that we would get back to the conditions of the 1930's, and those are the conditions under which they thrive.
At any rate, we find that the official opposition is now advocating the very same policies that were advocated and that were put into force by them during the 1930's. As I said, the leader of the official opposition has not said too much on the subject. However, when he was in the United Kingdom no doubt he spoke with greater confidence, and I find in the London Daily Express of October 8 of this year the following. This is in direct quotation marks, which indicates it is taken from the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, and it has to do with his policies. He says:
This is no new and strange idea. It would merely be a return to the situation which existed until 1939.
So that he is quite prepared, apparently, to return to the conditions of the 1930's, and is quite conscious that he is returning to those conditions. His other policy of advocating greater use, as he puts it, of resources within the country means, as was pointed out to him by a newspaperman in Manitoba, a restrictive policy to a certain degree. He denied that categorically. I read from the Winnipeg Free Press of October 31 an editorial entitled "Double Talk":
Mr. George Drew, speaking in this city Tuesday at a Conservative meeting, once more denied that he is advocating higher tariffs and a policy ol protection when he urges the greater use in domestic manufacture of our primary raw material. This is a distinction without a difference. What is worse, it is a refusal to identify his policy by its correct name.
I find that when the Leader of the Opposition went through Nipigon, Ontario, he also made a speech, and in explanation of what he meant by this policy he used an example

The Address-Mr. Jutras which I think illustrates the point very well. I quote from the Ottawa Journal of October 18, 1952:
Opposition Leader Drew yesterday indicated that conservation of resources for the primary use of Canadians will be an important plank In the Progressive Conservatives' general election platform.
Mr. Drew said the "manufacturing clause" in Ontario provincial legislation has ensured the processing of forest raw materials in areas where the people would benefit from employment and income in the north.
The clause restricted the export of unmanufactured forest products and ensured the continuance of pulp and paper mills around which have grown prosperous communities.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, whether there is a more striking example of the result that can be obtained from a policy of restriction of this nature. As a matter of fact, if you take that very industry, the paper industry in Canada, which is dependent upon markets outside of Canada to the extent of 90 per cent of its production, and apply any policy of restriction to it, and there is retaliation in other countries, it is easy to see in what position the industry would find itself in a very short time. It is quite obvious that once more the Leader of the Opposition has not yet outgrown his provincial outlook.
To justify this revival of this policy of the 1930's, the official opposition has drummed up the cry that we have lost our markets in Europe, that we have lost our markets in the commonwealth, and that we have lost our markets in the United Kingdom. Of course, the record is there and nothing could be farther from the truth. This is not new; this was the cry that they used in the 1945 election and they used it again in the 1949 election. We have had this repetitious cry ever since the end of the war, that we were losing markets. One does not have to analyse the statistics or even look at the record. It seems to me that the answer is quite obvious.
Since the end of the war our population has increased by 20 per cent. Sixteen billion dollars' worth of new capital expenditure has been poured into this country to expand production. As a matter of fact, the production of the country has increased by 100 per cent. It stands to reason that we must have found some markets outside, and that our export market must have expanded to take care of this 100 per cent increase in production, and at the same time permit the country to go through the greatest prosperity it has ever known. It is a matter of record indeed that the export trade of the country has gone up by 75 per cent since 1939, and as a result, as I just mentioned, we are going through a period of prosperity.
(Mr. Jutras.]

It is also a matter of record that at the present time a family of four earns one and a half times as much-and I mean in real terms-as it earned in 1939. The record of the figures of export trade speaks for itself.
When the Tory Conservative government turned over the reins of office to the Liberal party in 1935 the total export trade was in the neighbourhood of $700 million. This increased to over $3,000 million in 1948 and stood at $4,000 million in 1951, the last complete year for which we have statistics. As a matter of fact, there is every indication at the present time, according to the figures that are available, that this year will also be a record year so far as exports are concerned.
It is good to remember that under this policy they are advocating at the present time, this government took over a condition of unemployment, relief and despair throughout Canada in 1935. It is a matter of record that in less than a month the Liberal government signed a trade agreement with the United States, and this was followed by twenty trade agreements with twenty different countries, with the result, as statistics show, that there has been an increase and a betterment of conditions in the country gradually. May I say this for the benefit of those in the other corner, particularly those from western Canada. It is also a matter of record that by 1939, before the war, or from 1935 to 1939, the gross national income of the farmers of western Canada had increased by 90 per cent as a result of this policy of finding greater markets and expanding markets throughout the world and removing as many trade barriers as possible. It is also a matter of interest to wheat producers that when the Liberals left office in 1930 they left a carry-over in wheat of some 30 odd million bushels. When they resumed office four years later there was a carry-over of over 200 million bushels of wheat which, in those days, was considered an abnormally high carry-over, and no doubt exerted a downward pressure on the price of grain. The result was, as we know, that grain prices at that time were very low. This, again, indicates the effect of this type of policy.
I should like to apply the test of Liberal trade policies to the last grain crop of which w-e have record, namely, that of 1951-52. This crop was valued at $1,500 million, one of the most valuable we have had in this country. If we compare the value of that crop with the value of crude oil production in Canada, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) did in Toronto, which amounts to $120 million, we at once realize the importance of the western grain crop when it

reaches a figure of $1,500 million. And the current crop is expected to reach a figure of $1,800 million.
So that at the beginning of that crop year- just to show what the Department of Trade and Commerce was able to do, through the very able management of the minister of that department-we began that year with a carry-over of 190 million bushels. To that were added deliveries of 718 million bushels, making a total of close to a billion bushels of grain that had to be disposed of.
It must also be remembered that in that year out west the weather conditions were unsatisfactory in the fall. The grain that was delivered was in very poor condition. As a matter of fact 66 per cent of the crop was delivered in tough, damp or non-straight grades. The non-straight grades accounted for 66 per cent of the crops. About 100 million bushels had to be put through the driers, because it was not in a condition to be kept or shipped.
Despite these facts-and this is also a great tribute to the Canadian wheat board-despite these great difficulties, and the difficulty of movement, having in mind the fact that the grain cannot be hauled any great distance in that condition without heating or spoiling, it is a matter of record that, even under those very bad conditions, not a single bushel of grain was lost.
And so, Mr. Speaker, the board marketed 650 million bushels of grain, 141 million domestically and 509 million by export. This is the second highest export of grain in the history of the nation, despite all the difficulties I have mentioned, and the condition in which it was delivered.
The disposition of this export grain is also most revealing. Dealing first with the export of wheat and wheat flour, we find that the Department of Trade and Commerce sold wheat to 86 different countries in six continents of the world. They sold 386 million bushels of wheat, representing an export increase to the extent of 37 per cent over the previous year. That is not losing markets.
The distribution of that wheat is of special interest. I find that 63 per cent of the amount exported went to 20 countries in Europe

and I would ask the opposition to take note of that. Then 3 [DOT] 5 per cent went to 17 countries in Africa; 14 per cent to North America, 4-8 per cent to South America, and some smaller amounts to Oceania. Twenty-three areas of the commonwealth took 45 [DOT] 4 per cent. Then of course the United Kingdom, which is still the leading buyer, bought 127 -6 million bushels, or 36 per cent of the crop. That is a very large amount for
The Address-Mr. Jutras local consumption in the United Kingdom. Even the United States, which has a surplus of wheat, bought almost 39 million bushels from Canada.
Turning now to barley exports we find that the government exported 70 million bushels of barley, or three times the amount exported last year. This, too, is an all-time record, so far as the export of barley is concerned. It is of particular interest, too, to note that whereas formerly 80 per cent of the barley went to the United States, the biggest buyer of barley from the 1951-52 crop was in Europe. We sold to eight different countries. Belgium was the biggest buyer, with a purchase of 18 million bushels, Japan came next with 15 million, the United States 10 million, the United Kingdom 7-7 million, Germany 5 [DOT] 8 million, Denmark 3 [DOT] 3 million, The Netherlands 2 [DOT] 8 million and Norway 2 [DOT] 4 million.
The story is the same so far as the export of oats is concerned. There again 70 million bushels were exported, double the amount exported the year before', and again an alltime record. It went to ten different countries. Then, oatmeal and rolled oats were shipped to 26 countries. In connection with oats the United States was the biggest buyer with a total of 58 million bushels; Belgium was next with 8-3 million; and The Netherlands bought 1 [DOT] 8 million.
So that the total export of the five principal grains was 505-3 million bushels, again the highest export figure in the history of this nation. This grain was valued at $860 million, and represented 20 per cent of the total value of exports of the nation.
I hasten to point out that, in spite of these large exports of feed grains throughout the world, the domestic market was well cared for. As a matter of fact, there were left over 20 million tons of feed in Canada, which works out to roughly something more than one ton of feed to each feed-consuming animal in Canada. As a matter of fact this represents an increase of 33 per cent over the previous year.
Not only have markets been found outside Canada, but a local market, right within our boundaries, has been developed. Under the freight assistance program this new market has been developed right here in Canada. It is interesting to note that whereas the average amount of feed going to eastern Canada over the ten-year period from 1931 to 1940 was 12 million bushels per year, that figure has now increased to anywhere from 70 million to 75 million bushels per year. So that the increase is from 12 million to 70 million.
I wish therefore to tell hon. members from the east, from the maritime provinces, that

The Address-Mr. Jutras those of us in western Canada appreciate this market within Canada and we are ready to co-operate with them at all times in its development. Unfortunately when coarse grains were brought under the Canadian wheat board there was some criticism from feeders in eastern Canada who were a little disappointed in the way they were being affected. I warned them at the time that they were bound to be disappointed because I am afraid a great many supported the idea of the inclusion of coarse grains in the operations of the wheat board because they did not believe in such a system of marketing and were under the impression that the board would not be able to get the highest price and consequently they would get cheaper feeds.
Naturally they were caught short in their supplies in the first year and there was some criticism. I should like to place on the record the prices actually received by the farmer in western Canada for the feed sold in eastern Canada. I think upon a dose examination of the facts they will find that the fluctuations under this system of marketing were not as great nor was the margin as wide as some of them believed they would be.
Feed wheat No. 1 paid the western producer $1.49 basis Fort William, and the low on the market was $1.44 with the high being $1.56. It will be seen that the margin was not so great. No. 1 feed barley paid the western producer $1.21 basis Fort William, with the market in eastern Canada showing a low of $1.11 and a high of 1.48. Oats paid the producer 77 cents a bushel, with the market low being 77 cents and the high $1.08. It will be seen that the fluctuations and the disparity were not very great.
Attempts have been made to alleviate the situation and some time ago the western co-operatives suggested to Quebec, Ontario and the maritime provinces the setting up of a central buying agency to ensure supplies for eastern Canada. This appeared to be a sensible suggestion and it should work	to	the	advantage	of easternCanada. However, in a venture of this nature	the	first	requisite is a	staff of
competent and experienced men and there is a possibility there may be difficulty in getting such staff.
In order to show their good faith the western co-operatives offered to pay 50 per cent of any losses during the first year of operation up to $100,000. That offer is still pending and it may help to smooth out the differences between the east and the west.
I believe that this marketing policy has worked to the advantage of the eastern and western provinces. It has eliminated some
rMr. Jutras.]

of the fluctuations and while the western producer has not received the highest prices he feels that he is getting a reasonable and fair price when all factors are taken into consideration.
I have attempted to analyse the export situation in connection with this mainstay of western agriculture and I think I have demonstrated that not only have we not lost world markets, we have constantly expanded' our markets throughout the world. The history and experience of this country indicates that that is the only way we can ensure prosperity. We should trade as much as possible with every country in the world and build up markets wherever they can be found so that there may be a greater demand for Canadian products.
The record shows that not only has the Liberal government attempted to get greater markets for Canadian products, they have endeavoured on every occasion to enlarge the markets of other nations. That is why we have joined in these various international agreements which I think should remain in effect. We have attempted to reduce trade barriers and we have concentrated on expanding the trade of this country, thus increasing our standard of living. Any government that would adopt restrictive practices or even mention that they contemplated adopting such policies would do great damage to the economy of the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose at this time to draw attention to the war in Korea and Canada's part therein. The speech from the throne contains the following:
The sacrifices of those directly involved in the United Nations police action in Korea and the anxieties of their families are an inevitable and most regrettable part of the price we are paying to prevent another world war.
I am sure that we all want to express our sympathy to the families that have been bereaved and to the men who have been wounded.
I notice that the Canadian casualty lists show a steady increase and the seriousness of the war can be gauged from these lists. The casualty list dated Ottawa, November 23, and sent out by Canadian Press was as follows:
A Korean casualty list Saturday included four men killed in action and one officer and six men wounded.
The list brought to 1,234 total casualties suffered by Canadian troops in Korea, including 231 dead, 890 wounded, 28 missing, 84 injured in action and one captured.
The navy has reported three dead and three injured.
That was the 153rd casualty list that had been issued. On May 12 of this year the 108th

casualty list was issued and showed the total number of casualties at that time as 784. In the six months from May to November 23 the increase has been 88 killed, 319 wounded and 20 missing. As an indication of the increasing seriousness of the war in Korea I should like to refer to the casualty lists in this way: In the first nine months since the brigade was in Korea the casualties were at the rate of 42 per month; in the following seven months the rate was 58 per month; in the last six months, that is from May to November of this year, the rate was 75 per month.
How serious are our casualties in Korea in comparison with other wars? In the first place, casualties should be shown as a percentage of the fighting troops, not of the total enlistment. Only in this way can a true picture be obtained. For every man who is actively engaged with the enemy there are at least four who are in the rear areas or on the lines of communication. The heaviest casualties are suffered by the infantry. In world war I, according to the casualty figures shown in the memorial chamber of this building, the infantry who were in France and Flanders suffered 68 per cent of the total casualties.
Consider the casualty list of Dieppe. In that action 5,000 Canadians participated. Six infantry battalions and other formations landed on the beaches and all non-fighting personnel of each unit had been left in England. Dead and wounded were approximately 3,000, or 60 per cent of the total fighting strength of the Dieppe force.
In Korea we have a brigade consisting of supporting units and of three infantry battalions: the Royal Canadian Regiment, the Royal 22nd Regiment and the Princess Patricia's Canadian Eight Infantry. The front line fighting strength of each battalion may be estimated at 600, or 1,800 for the three battalions. On these men has fallen the brunt of the fighting and of the casualties.
The total battle casualties, if we omit those listed as injured or captured, amount to 1,149 and of that number I am assuming most are infantry men for I have not the figures for the tanks, signals, engineers or artillery. Had there been no rotation of battalions and had the original brigade remained in Korea from February of 1951 to the present time without replacement, the fighting strength of the brigade would now be one battalion, not three.
In other words, the casualties have been approximately 68 per cent, the same heavy casualty rate as at Dieppe. The only difference is that at Dieppe the casualty rate of 60 per cent was suffered in a period of nine hours and the casualty rate of 68 per cent in Korea has been spread over 22 months.
The Address-Mr. Churchill This is not a police action in Korea; it is war, with all its horrors, its suffering, and its bloodshed.
On November 25, I asked a question of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) in these words as given in Hansard at page 63:
. . . are tanks used by Canadian forces in Korea so short of ammunition that they are permitted to fire only two shells per tank per day?
The minister replied in these words:
... I can say that during relatively static periods on any battlefront ammunition is rationed in the sense that guns of all types are allowed a certain number of rounds per day. That is so that they can build up stocks either to meet an attack or, in this case, to meet the possible contingency of an ultimate armistice. We. certainly are not going to give the number of rounds per day that are to be fired by any Canadian artillery until they have been fired. The hon. member knows very well indeed that it would be highly improper to do so even if it referred only to the Canadian forces. But in this case our ammunition is supplied from United States sources. We are on the United States supply line and get precisely the same treatment as the Americans get. I am sure that the American military authorities in the United Nations would be the first to refuse this information.
I was not asking for a disclosure as to the number of rounds that might be fired each day by the artillery. I was inquiring whether there was a shortage of ammunition. My experience would lead me to conclude that a ration of two shells per gun per day means there is a shortage of ammunition.
I think you would have to go back to the year 1915 to discover a parallel to this situation. In May of 1915, according to the British official history of the war, very frequently battles had to be brought to a conclusion because of a scarcity of ammunition; and the common phrase used in the order was "the battle must now cease". You will find that expression in the official history of the war, 1915, page 37. A cessation of hostilities due to lack of ammunition occurred at the battle of Festubert in which Canadian forces were engaged.
It might be appropriate at this stage to mention that the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry first battalion, which has just returned from Korea, has had a casualty list of 36 killed, 2 missing believed killed, and 196 wounded-a total of 236 casualties in eleven months of service in Korea. The original Princess Patricia's serving in France in May of 1915, at the time of this shortage of ammunition, suffered very severely during a twenty-four hour period from the evening of May 7 until the evening of May 8. Six hundred and thirty-five men of the original Patricia's answered the roll call on the 7th of May. When they were relieved on the night of the 8th they mustered only 150.
330	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Churchill
At that particular time, in May, 1915, a dispatch was published in the London Times dated May 12, from the Times correspondent in France in these words, and I quote:
The want of an unlimited supply of high explosives was a fatal bar to our success.
That dispatch resulted in editorials in the newspapers, the stirring up of public interest in the question, the organization of a ministry of munitions, the appointment of Lloyd George as the head of that department, and a general increase in the production of ammunition. If a shortage of ammunition in May, 1915, resulted in that type of attention and action, what about the situation we are facing today?
My question was based on a Canadian Press dispatch from Tokyo which appeared in the Globe and Mail about ten days or perhaps two weeks ago. The last paragraph reads as follows:
Bill Boss, Canadian Press correspondent in Korea, reported today that the tanks are allowed to fire only two shells a day apiece from their 76 mm. main guns and quoted one officer as saying that, "rationed as we are, we've had to pass up targets galore".
I discovered subsequently that the full dispatch had not been printed in that paper but had appeared in the Calgary Herald. It went on to say they were not permitted to use their machine gun ammunition from the tanks except in case of enemy attack.
There are two sentences in the minister's reply to my question which deserve attention. Speaking of the rationing of ammunition he said, and I quote:
That is so that they can build up stocks either to meet an attack or, as In this case, to meet the possible contingency of an ultimate armistice.
I fail to understand what is meant by "to meet the possible contingency of an ultimate armistice". Does that mean that artillery fire should be kept to a minimum while armistice negotiations are continuing, in order not to exasperate the enemy? If that is the case, why fire at all? If you do not harass the enemy with fire he is free to make all manner of preparations on his side for a surprise attack. If our gunners are passing up targets galore, the enemy is obviously being very bold and very active.
Armistice negotiations have been going on for the last seventeen months, and for at least the last six months the point at issue has been narrowed down to a method of exchanging prisoners; but the armistice still lurks around the corner. During the last six months Canadian casualties have been 88 killed, 319 wounded, 22 missing, or a total of 429. We suffer 429 casualties, and yet restrict


harassing fire on the enemy while we await an armistice. No army could fight under those conditions. Forces in contact with the enemy cannot be looking over their shoulder for the dove of peace without running the risk of being surprised by the enemy. Let us recall the German attack on the Ardennes in December, 1944, a very critical period in the last war.
In November, 1918, every soldier in the Canadian army knew an armistice was expected at any moment. Was there any let-up in the relentless drive of the Canadian corps? On the morning of November 11, Canadian troops continued to advance, and those who were in support were warned to be ready to leapfrog the forward troops and push onward if necessary on the 12th. There was no rationing of ammunition in those days to meet the possible contingency of an armistice. In May, 1945, every soldier in the Canadian army knew that German resistance was on the point of collapsing. Yet, on the 4th of May we find, and I quote the official historian:
. . . divisions of the second Canadian corps were still advancing northward and still meeting opposition.
That is found in "The Canadian Army, 1939-45", page 270. As late as noon of that day, impending attacks by Canadians were cancelled by the army commander on instructions from General Montgomery's headquarters because the German surrender was at that time being negotiated and was about to be signed, as it was the same day. There had been no rationing of ammunition down to two shells per gun per day.
The second sentence in the minister's reply, to which close attention should be given, reads as follows:
We are on the United States supply line, and get precisely the same treatment as the Americans get.
I suppose the minister would include the South Koreans. In other words, if there is a restriction on the use of ammunition or a shortage of ammunition all formations in the army in Korea get the same treatment.
At this point, it would be interesting to refer to another dispatch from Korea, and again I am indebted to the Ottawa Citizen of November 24. This dispatch is from the Kumhwa front, Korea, and the headline reads: "Allied officers sick at heart; appalling loss of men in fighting for Kumhwa." The dispatch describes the attack by the Korean second division on Sniper ridge and by the United States seventh division on Triangle hill. The battle commenced on October 14. On October 24, the Koreans relieved the United States division. The Chinese counterattacked on October 31 and overran Triangle,

inflicting heavy casualties on troops who refused to retreat. Then the dispatch reads as follows:
The allied situation at this point was made extremely difficult by restrictions that cut back sharply the rate of allied artillery fire in order to save shells.
This paralyzing order came just as the communists completed the massing of more than 200 field guns and thousands of mortars on the front.
Then the high command, appalled at the communist fire power, threw economy to the winds and poured guns and shells into the sector in the greatest artillery mobilization since the second world war.
Had the commonwealth division taken over Sniper ridge and Triangle hill from the U.S. seventh division, we would now be mourning the annihilation of the Canadian 25th brigade because of a paralysing order to cut back the rate of artillery fire in order to save shells. If the 25th Canadian brigade is involved in a major action in December, will there be ammunition available against counter-attack? Is there a shortage of ammunition in Korea? There is no secrecy or security involved in this matter because these dispatches have informed the world that all is not well on the allied side in Korea.
What is the nature of the Korean conflict? General Van Fleet, commander-in-chief of the eighth army, has given the answer in an article reprinted in part in the Ottawa Citizen of November 24. He was commenting on the increased use of South Korean troops and their employment with allied forces, and considered this arrangement suitable-I give his words-"for the type of defensive warfare in which we are engaged-static positions with little movement in mountainous terrain". That is the Korean picture; a mountainous country, with the armies deadlocked in static positions and the emphasis on defence. It is not a repetition of world war II but of world war I.
The terrain precludes the continuous trench system of the western front system of 1914-18, but obviously favours the fortification of mountain strongholds. It is generally accepted that, under these conditions, the defenders are more favourably situated than the attackers. With observation posts in the hills and sufficient fire power available, the passes through the hills can be denied the enemy without the necessity of actually occupying the low ground with troops. Veterans of the Italian campaign would recognize, I assume, many similarities in the Korean battlefront. Monte Cassino, the anchor of the Gustav line of defence in Italy, is an example of the value and strength of a fortified hill position. Consider Vimy Ridge of the first world war. It 68108-221	i .	|
The Address-Mr. Churchill was not a mountain, of course, but a commanding hill position. Fortified by the Germans it was proof against all attack during 1915 and 1916, and cost the lives of 50,000 Frenchmen. This position was taken only by a major assault in 1917.
If our military plan in Korea is to remain on the defensive, and I think it should be, if the warfare is static and not mobile, then I should like to know something about the nature of our defensive preparations. My observation has been that under static conditions of warfare there is every opportunity to establish enormous dumps of ammunition. It is under mobile conditions that supply lines tend to break down and that restrictions on the use of ammunition have to be imposed. Look at the situation in which we find ourselves. There is no submarine menace; we have an airlift and the railway system in Korea is functioning. There are 38 trams daily moving from Pusan to Seoul. They have 60 modern diesels, 360 steam locomotives, and we have air supremacy to protect our supply lines. We have the industrial capacity of the North American continent, and still we are told by correspondents in Korea that there is a shortage of ammunition under these static conditions.
Now, someone may say that I am trespassing on the forbidden ground of the higher military command. My answer is that if the reports are authentic about a shortage of ammunition in Korea or of restrictions on the use of ammunition, even in the face of enemy attacks, then a complete explanation of the conduct and direction of the Korean war should be given to parliament without delay. Have we anything to say as a Canadian nation in regard to the conduct and direction of the war in Korea? A few months ago some concern was expressed about the employment of Canadian troops at the prisoner of war camps. Has anything yet been said about the ammunition supply in Korea or about the methods of defence? These seem to me to be of much greater importance.
What is our military position in Korea? Have we sent merely token forces to meet our obligation as a member of the United Nations? Have we given hostages to fortune? What is our means of communication with the commander of the eighth army? If our 25th brigade should be assigned a role in Korea that, in the opinion of our brigade commander, would result in needless loss of life, has our brigadier any authority to raise objection? Have we at eighth army headquarters any Canadian officer of sufficiently

The Address-Mr. Churchill high rank to influence decisions? The British have a major-general as liaison officer with the United Nations staff in Korea.
We have now two major commitments abroad, namely, in Korea and in Europe. In the future, we may face other commitments of an international nature. How are we protecting Canadian interests under these circumstances?
These questions are not academic. Military doctrine and military methods differ. Continental powers with large populations, such as Russia, Germany and the United States, have tended to be more prodigal in their use of manpower than have Great Britain and Canada. Profiting by the lessons of world war I, the commonwealth armies husbanded their manpower and used armoured vehicles and unlimited supplies of ammunition. The result was only one-third as many casualties as in the first war.
General Montgomery was criticized by some people for what they called overinsurance. General Montgomery believed in expending ammunition, not men. So did General Crerar. On February 8, 1945, when the assault by British and Canadian troops was launched against the Reichwalde forest and the Siegfried line, the artillery under his command fired 160,000 shells just in a few hours.
What is the policy in Korea? If my information is correct, United States military teaching has emphasized attack and has paid less attention to defence and withdrawal. British and Canadian military instruction has given much greater emphasis to defence and withdrawal, owing to wide experience with expeditionary forces fighting against superior numbers; and we are fighting against superior numbers in Korea. We are supposed to be on the defensive. How effective is our line of defence? The 155-mile front has its flanks on the sea. We cannot be outflanked. Sixty per cent of the line is held by South Koreans, 25 per cent by United States troops, and 15 per cent by other United Nations forces including, of course, the commonwealth division and our Canadian brigade. We should be able to resist a frontal attack. The only course then open to the enemy who cannot outflank you is, under these circumstances, an airborne assault behind our front line. But we have air superiority which effectively prevents an airborne attack.
After seventeen months of static warfare, are we so dug in in depth that the enemy cannot effect a penetration of our lines? Is our defensive fire plan so effective that we cannot be surprised? It does not appear so.
The third battalion of the Princess Patricia's is now in Korea. Its first task, its initiation


into warfare, was to counter-attack, to assist the Black Watch, who had been overrun. Canada then issued its 153rd casualty list. Yet in the Globe and Mail of November 28 I read that two Chinese attacks on Sniper ridge on November 27 had failed because allied defensive fire was intense and accurate. The question that arises in my mind is this: What was the defensive fire plan on the commonwealth division front? Were our troops short of ammunition?
In fact, the whole plan of defence in Korea puzzles me. Are our troops still eking out an existence in foxholes? Do we need an organization in Korea similar in purpose to the German Todt group to build defensive lines of permanence that provide full protection for the troops and that are proof against anything except an all-out major effort? Consider the German defences in Italy in the recent war. They had three substantial defence lines. They had the Gustav line, the Adolf Hitler line and the Caesar line. Our official historian, Colonel Stacey, in dealing with this matter says of the Hitler line:
The line depended for its strength upon a formidable barrier of concrete and steel structures ... a number of these were miniature fortresses . . . and each was flanked by additional anti-tank guns manned by crews whose living quarters were secure concrete burrows twenty feet below ground.
Of the Gustav line he says:
On the German side carefully sited weapon positions on the valley floor and in the mountains to north and south permitted the enemy to sweep the whole of the fortified zone with fire, while deep shelters protected the defenders against our air and artillery bombardment.
One can think of other lines of defence such as the Atlantic wall, the Siegfried line of 1939-45 and the Hindenburg line of 1917-18. These are all examples of the art of defence, where the defender has an adequate zone of fire and has adequate protection for the men who are in this defensive position.
What are we relying upon in Korea? Are we relying on concrete gun emplacements, pill-boxes, mine fields and barbed wire or are we relying upon air power and counterattacks by infantry?
Reports from Korea indicate that the Chinese have increased appreciably the number of their mortars and guns. Have we done the same? If not, are we planning to do so? Should we not now double the artillery component of the brigade, increase the mortars, and add more heavy machine guns? For defensive static warfare, these are the weapons. Have we the multiple rocket projector in Korea? Its effect was devastating in northwest Europe. Should we double our tank strength? No great increase in personnel will be required to do this, but even if there were

sn increase in artillery personnel, for example, we would save on casualties that are inflicted on the infantry.
The experience of the two great wars has been that each successive year there was an increase in the fire power of the opposing armies. More guns and more ammunition were available. Part of the success of the Canadian corps in 1917 and 1918 was due to the fact that it had more artillery pieces and more machine guns than had other corps. Its machine gun strength was doubled in 1918 almost overnight. Under static conditions, with guns properly sited and with observation posts established, the Canadian corps was impregnable. At the battle of Hill 70 in the summer of 1917, the Germans launched 13 counter-attacks. Each counter-attack was destroyed by artillery and machine gun fire. Not one German reached our front line despite these desperate efforts. Cannot the same methods be used and similar results be achieved in Korea? The lesson of the war of 1914-18 is that men unaided by tanks simply cannot make an effective break-through by frontal attack. Not even Chinese are proof against artillery and mortar and machine-gun fire. Fire power rather than counterattacks by infantry should be the defensive plan in Korea.
Another problem arises. Is the war in Korea now being considered as a war of attrition? I have seen several articles that have suggested that the Chinese cannot long endure the heavy losses they have suffered. Some Canadian officers, in conversation with me, have ventured the same opinion. There are at least three things wrong with this opinion. In the first place, the estimates of Chinese casualties have been grossly exaggerated. If they were true, General Van Fleet says: "There wouldn't be a live Chinese or North Korean opposing us." You will find that quotation on page 39 of the Reader's Digest for December. In the second place, a war of attrition against an enemy whose population exceeds 400 million is simply ridiculous. In the third place, the concept of the war of attrition by means of offensive action was applied in 1916 and 1917 with grievous effect to the wrong side; for the casualty lists published after that war showed that the allies had suffered greater losses than had the Germans in those very years when the military commanders were claiming that Germany's lifeblood was being drained away. And we of the British commonwealth expended 250,000 lives in the Ypres salient alone. War by attrition does not necessarily affect the other side.
The Address-Mr. Churchill
I suggest to the Minister of National Defence that for the instruction of our present generation of military officers we proceed rapidly with the official history of world war I. Our competent official historian will be able to deduce many a lesson on the effective use of fire power against superior numbers and on the tactics of defence under static conditions. These lessons will be valuable for officers whose practical experience has been only with mobile forces in the advance, efficient as they proved themselves to be under those circumstances.
There need be no conflict between politicians and military leaders in those matters. I am putting forward various suggestions in the hope of obtaining the type of information that I think should be available to parliament. I am in agreement with the minister. He is already on record in Hansard of 1952, volume I, page 1080. These are his words:
When we have men in battle facing a foe abroad we put above everything else the necessity of supporting, in every way, those men who are risking and giving their lives in order that peace may be restored and freedom preserved.
How do we support these men in every way, these men who are risking their lives? We must support them by having some part in determining the conduct of the war in Korea. Canadian military experience is, at the very least, the equal of United States military experience. Is Canadian military experience playing a part on the higher levels in the Korean conflict? We must support these men by providing the arms and ammunition. In the third year of any war, there should be not a trickle but a flood of ammunition. We must support them with adequate fully-trained replacements. Will the minister assure the house that that is being done? We must support them by retaining effective political control over our forces and not relinquishing that control to the military. That is in the British and Canadian tradition. What assurance can the minister give us on that point?
What is the future in Korea? For those who are interested in the subject-and I imagine every member of the House of Commons is-may I suggest that they will find a brief and well written survey in the International Journal of the autumn of 1952 by G. H. Stanley, who is at the Royal Military College at Kingston. In the last issue of the U. S. News and World Report, which is dated December 5, there is a good summary of the Korean situation, and the various proposals are there balanced one against the other. I have no time to go into that, but I do suggest that parliament should seriously consider Canada's position with regard to decisions that may be made in connection

The Address-Mr. Croll with the war in Korea, because on those decisions depend a great many things and the lives of our soldiers may be at stake.
For our Canadian forces in Korea I have nothing but admiration-for their courage and for their devotion 1o duty. They are Canadians; it follows that they have no superiors on the battlefield. I hope that the fortune of war will not strike down any one of our battalions as the Gloucesters were struck down. Should our brigade be called upon to storm a ridge like Sniper ridge or Triangle hill, and hold it without sufficient artillery support, I am confident that they will face their hour of trial with fortitude and determination.
We are engaged in Korea not in a police action but in a war. We have lost the equivalent of the fighting strength of two battalions. We are calling upon our young men to sacrifice their lives on the field of battle thousands of miles from home. Are we taking every precaution to see that. not one of those lives is needlessly lost?

speechtext:
This house is fully aware that national health insurance ranks high on the government's list of unfinished business. It is the next great step towards social security. I think that it affects every one of Canada's 14,009,429 people, and I would not be exaggerating if I said that it is a matter of life and death for some of the people of this country.
If you are a wage earner with dependents you are all right until you get sick and then you are licked. The subject of health insurance is scarcely a new one. It has to my personal knowledge been discussed and debated in the house at least since 1945, and it was by no means a new subject then.
It may be of interest if I recall to hon. members that today there are 39 countries in the world that have national health insurance plans. Most of them provide not only for medical but also for hospital services. Many of them provide for sickness and maternity benefits. Lest there should be anyone in this house who thinks that only socialist Britain and Soviet Russia have taken this step, I want to point out that the other countries include Sweden and Norway, Denmark, Iceland, New Zealand, Guatemala and even little Panama. Nor is health insurance a post-war freak, for the earliest scheme of health insurance was set up in Austria in 1883, almost 70 years ago. It is only fair to say that these schemes are by no means perfect or Utopian. All observers who have had an opportunity to view these health plans admit that they are handicapped by shortages of technical staffs and hospital facilities. But


that does not deter those countries from setting up health insurance plans. It is significant that in every country where a health insurance plan has been set up it has acted as a spur to hospital expansion, encouraging and accelerating building and medical facilities.
In Britain, to take only one recent example, the number of doctors, nurses and laboratory technicians has increased faster since the health plan was set up in 1948 than ever before. We find that Canada is behind many countries in providing adequate health care at costs which the people can afford. A nation with the second highest standard of living is twelfth in infant mortality rate.

speechtext:
Let me read you just a few
health statistics which will help us to understand the problem that is involved. Every year in Canada the following deaths occur because of sickness and disease: Tuberculosis, in 1950, 3,583; in 1951, 3,418; communicable diseases, in 1950, 5,577; in 1951, 6,999; infants under one year, 15,324 in 1950 and 14,584 in 1951; infants at birth, under one day, 3,996 in 1950 and 3,637 in 1951.
Here we have nearly 30,000 deaths a year, most of which are caused by lack of proper living conditions and medical care. Just think of it! Thirty thousand people die every year, more than a quarter of a million every ten years, and most of the deaths could have been prevented.
Nor is my list of statistics complete by any means. Let me recall some figures that were given the house several years ago by a former minister of labour. He pointed out that out of 1,014,491 men examined under mobilization regulations 55 per cent were unfit for front-line service and 285,055 were unfit for service anywhere, in any capacity.
I have here a report contained in the Ottawa Journal of November 12, 1952, in which Lieutenant Colonel H. V. Matthews of Toronto, speaking before an armistice gathering in Kitchener, said:
More than 50 per cent of the youths trying to enlist in Canada are unfit for military service. We reject more people than we accept.
In other words, out of more than a million Canadians examined, more than half had health defects which made them unfit for military service. These figures are only for men of military age. What about the women and children, and the older people? We can assume that these shocking figures can be projected across the entire population of this country. A balance sheet of national health would contain a staggering figure of human lives lost or impaired, of millions of manhours los4, of untold pain and suffering and

sickness. The net result is a wastage of human life, manpower and money which dwarfs understanding.
Faced with this appalling balance sheet of health, no one person in the House of Commons or in the country will deny that everything possible must be done to help remedy the situation. There is of course no simple prescription for national health. It is compounded of many ingredients, and there may not be general agreement on all of them. But one vital ingredient is beyond dispute: It is simply this, a better distribution of all health services. No prescription for national health which does not include this can possibly be effective. We must find the means of providing better health for all, regardless of ability to pay. We must remove the price tag from health, and share the cost of illness. We must make sure that economic needs do not prevent Canadians from having access to the health care they need. Patients must have the right to choose their doctors, and the doctor his patients. Doctors are not to be servants of the state, but are to be free to serve their patients.
I am just as much opposed to socialized medicine as is any doctor. I do not want to see our doctors on the government payroll. But we need the help and guidance of the medical profession in a constructive spirit to help solve our problem. In common with many others in this country I believe our answer is to be found in some plan of national health insurance underwritten by the dominion and administered by the provinces for the benefit of all Canadians.
I am well aware there are some objections to national health insurance. I suppose the first objection is that our medical facilities in Canada are not developed sufficiently to support a comprehensive plan of national health insurance. That may well be true. But let us not lose sight of a few things. First, I do not believe our medical facilities are less either in quantity or in quality than those of most other civilized nations. I know that our doctors, our nurses and our technical people are second to none in the world. I know of few countries that can boast finer or better equipped hospitals or clinics.
No doubt it may be said, and with truth, that we have not enough of these things. But what country has? I do not wish to make unfavourable comparisons with any other country; but I would ask whether Canada is in any worse position medically speaking than Norway, New Zealand or Panama. I cannot believe it. Yet these small nations are among the 39 which have introduced national health insurance.
The Address-Mr. Croll
Of course we have not enough medical and health facilities; no country has. But if we are going to sit back and wait until we do, then you know when we are going to get health insurance: just about never. I am convinced that greater health facilities will come with a health insurance plan. That has been the experience of every country that has adopted such a plan; and it is significant that in no country was a plan abandoned because facilities proved unequal to the task.
Today we may lack personnel and facilities which are deemed sufficient; but is that a good enough reason for not starting a plan, even in a limited fashion? It just cannot be argued that a country as rich as we are cannot bed down its sick and remove from its people the constant fear that illness may strike their homes tomorrow and throw them on charity.
The next objection of course may come from members of the medical profession. It is regrettable that the subject of national health insurance should be viewed with such suspicion, alarm-and worse-by a considerable number of Canadian doctors. Yet such is the case. The stock reply we get from the doctor is: Why should I become a civil servant? This feeling, which I call civil service phobia, dies very hard. Leaving aside for the moment the slander against civil servants, whom I personally have found to be diligent and conscientious, I believe that this reaction from a portion of the medical profession betrays a lack of understanding of the whole subject of health insurance.
I do not suggest that doctors are not fully aware of the need for expanded health services. No one has better opportunity than has the doctor, who meets the problem a hundred times a day. But I feel the medical profession are under a misconception of the true meaning and purpose of national health insurance. No one is proposing to take away from the doctor or the patient freedom of choice in their dealings one with the other. No one is proposing to make doctors civil servants or to turn patients into slaves of a bureaucratic medical system. By our administration of social services in this country we have amply demonstrated that we can have welfare without tyranny. Another objection to health insurance doubtless will be its cost. I can only ask hon. members to refer to the health figures I quoted earlier.
This country cannot afford to be without health insurance. Of course health insurance cannot be had for nothing. We must not mislead either the people or ourselves on that score at this stage of our thinking on the subject. I do not think that anyone can do
336	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Croll any more than hazard a guess as to the cost. It depends upon the extent of the plan and one thing is sure: the more extensive, the more expensive. I say again: Can we afford to be without health insurance? Once that question is answered we can go on to examine the problem of the cost. The Toronto Star of February 15,1950, contained the following:
Public medical care programs for persons receiving public assistance are now in operation in four provinces. Ontario was the first to establish, in 1935, a public medical service for persons on relief. In 1942 the service was extended to old age pensioners and families receiving mothers' allowance. In 1943, Saskatchewan put into operation a more generous medical care service for all recipients of public assistance, and since 1947 similar programs were put into effect by the governments of Alberta and British Columbia.
These programs are helping to build experience and to train administrators of health insurance in Canada.
I quote that because I happen to know something of that problem. I am no great authority on health insurance, but the house will be interested to know that as minister of welfare for Ontario in 1935 it was my responsibility to look after the people who were victims of the depression. At that time one in ten residents of Ontario needed medical care. Acting in my capacity as minister in consultation with the medical association we found a formula that provided medical care for those people on a fee-for-service basis. We paid the medical association which in turn paid the doctors. This was the first province-wide health plan in Canada. As the article indicates, that plan has been continued in Ontario as a model arrangement. In 1942 it was extended to old age pensioners and those receiving family allowances. It was copied in 1945 in Saskatchewan, and in 1947 by the Alberta and British Columbia governments.
As a supporter of health insurance and as an innovator, I have some appreciation of the administrative problems involved. I think I have some idea of the intimate and precise study and preparation required before we can take the next step.
Before I say anything further may I indicate to the house that I had the privilege of hearing the report by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Time did not permit him to relate more than a small portion of the achievements of that department, and they are many and great. The government's record on health and welfare must be described in glowing terms. I support what has already been done and I associate myself with its accomplishments. The minister has
[Mr. Croll.1

been consistently an advocate of health insurance. He has been intimately concerned with the sick and the ill. It may be that he thinks he has moved as fast as circumstances and conditions will permit. I think he is moving a little slowly. For that reason I am prepared to push him, but I am not prepared to shove him.
Let us see what courses are open to us. The government could present a bill on health insurance, we could debate and criticize it, and as a government measure it would have to pass. I do not think anyone in this house suggests that that course of action should be adopted. On the other hand, the minister could present a bill on national health insurance, its principle could be adopted, and then the bill could be referred to a committee of this house or to a joint committee of both houses to consider and report back. In that case the committee would be limited to making inquiries within the scope of the bill. I do not think that that is good enough.
Then the government could appoint a committee of this house or a joint committee with wide powers to study health insurance in the light of modern needs, conditions and accomplishments, with instructions to bring in a report which the government might or might not adopt in part or in whole. I think that that is the proper course to follow. I ask the government to set up at this session a joint committee of both houses to prepare a blueprint for national health insurance.
We in this house know very little about health insurance; the public knows even less. The public feel that they need it, they want it, but they are not quite sure what it will entail. They have a feeling it would be for their good. There has been a great deal of talk in the house about the number of studies that have been carried on, but the fact is that only two studies of this problem have been made in the last twenty-five years. I cannot emphasize that too strongly.
In 1928 the standing committee on industrial and international relations investigated insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity and brought in two reports. On June 1, 1928, they brought in a report dealing with the legislative jurisdiction, and I quote:
That the evidence of the justice department makes it clear that the responsibility for such legislation rests on the provincial authorities, it being within their jurisdiction under the provisions of the British North America Act; but that it would be within the power of parliament to contribute by grant to such provinces as adopted such legislation, following the precedents set in the matter of technical education, highway construction, and. more recently, the Old Age Pensions Act.

The Address-Mr. Croll
On May 1, 1929, the same committee Drought in a further recommendation as follows:
That with regard to sickness insurance, the Department of Pensions and National Health be requested to initiate a comprehensive survey of the field of public health, with special reference to a national health program. In tnis, it is believed that it would be possible to secure the co-operation of the provincial and municipal health departments, as well as the organized profession.
That date of May 1, 1929, is significant. Everyone remembers the hungry thirties. At the end of the thirties we entered a war and we did not come out of it until 1945. It is significant that in 1948 definite steps were taken, not only to comply with this recommendation but to go even beyond the recommendation.
In 1943 we had a special committee on health composed of top civil servants which was known as the Heagerty committee. They did a very able job, but the Heagerty report is now ten years old. We are living in the penicillin age. Scientific progress has been rapid in recent years and the demand for better care and the cost of providing it have both increased sharply. We are faced with a whole new set of problems in the field of health. Surely the friends of health insurance recognize the need for an up-to-date study by members of this house.
The impression is often given here that the British introduced their health scheme overnight. No such thing. A parliamentary committee studied it and brought in a report; and they had before them the Beveridge report which has used it as the basis for recommending the present health plan. Then I hear many people say: Oh, you have been promising it since 1919. That is true. Does it ever occur to those who make the statement that this is not an overnight project? It was 1911 when Lloyd George first introduced health and unemployment insurance in Great Britain but it was 37 years later when the act came into effect. It was 1912 when Teddy Roosevelt, not Franklin, first suggested health insurance in the United States. They still have not got it. The last report was made on health insurance following a request by President Truman in September of 1948, a significant year because we did something about health at the same time. President Truman wrote to Oscar Ewing, who was the federal security administrator, and asked him to make a survey; and Mr. Ewing did so. He told the President there were four phases to health insurance, and I quote from page 91 of
"The Nation's Health-A Ten-year Program". This is a United States government publication.
Phase one
Federal legislation to settle the basic policies of a system of government insurance and to decide important details; and to provide for a three-year "tooling-up" period before the date on which insurance benefits are made available.
Phase two
The tooling-up period during which procedures would be worked out co-operatively by professional groups, localities, states and the federal government; agreements arrived at with individuals and groups providing medical services; and the machinery for actual operations set up.
Phase three
Operations begin, services are provided up to the ceiling set by resources as they exist at the time.
Phase four
Expansion of services, as the accelerated increase and improved distribution of medical manpower and facilities lift the ceiling, until comprehensive services are available to everyone, everywhere in the country.
Mr. Ewing further told the President that would take ten years.
I think it would be unfair to the members of this house and it would be hazardous to the public to ask us to inaugurate a comprehensive insurance plan until we have much more information. Let us just deal with the question of cost for a few minutes. It has been suggested by a group in the house that the cost is likely to be $30 per capita. The minister has made the suggestion that it is likely to be $43 per capita, and the voluntary agencies suggest that $50 is a better figure. If for a family of three the cost will be approximately $12 a month, how is it to be paid? Is it to be paid entirely by the employer or by the employee, or is there to be a division? Is it to be a flat rate or a graduated rate or a combination of flat and graduated? What will be the government contribution?
Should we not know something about what has been done with the $160 million that we appropriated in 1948 which was for a five-year health grants program? How much of that has been committed? How much has been spent? How many new beds have resulted from construction? How are they distributed? How many people have they trained professionally?
What about the attitude of the provincial government? Should we not give detailed study to the provincial surveys? They have gone to a lot of trouble. Would I be wrong if I said that no one in this house has read them? Would we not be subject to very serious criticism if we did not first read the surveys and find out where the provinces stand?

The Address-Mr. Croll
I have a report from the Windsor Star dated October 24 which deals with the provincial attitudes to health insurance. It reads:
. . . Newfoundland has not yet reported . . . Ontario and Quebec did not comment . . . British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan are strongly in favour of some such plan. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island are satisfied for the time being to leave it to the voluntary plans. New Brunswick, while seeing both advantages and disadvantages, . . . seems to oppose an immediate start. Manitoba favours health insurance in principle but feels that it is not feasible at the present time.
Not much comfort there. What about the private agencies? How many persons are covered by the voluntary agencies such as Blue Cross, physicians' service, insurance companies and co-operative organizations? Some employers at the present time are obligated to pay a portion of the employees' cost of health insurance. Will that obligation carry on if the voluntary agencies are integrated or taken over? Should the plan be an over-all plan or should health insurance be introduced progressively? As far as I am concerned, I can take my health insurance without wigs, toupees or false teeth on the first day it starts.
Is not a joint committee the proper place to study other health plans, to compare costs, question witnesses, arid give public bodies a chance to be heard? Will it not also be of educational value to the people of Canada in the interests of a clear understanding of what is involved?
Dr. Malcolm G. Taylor, director of the Saskatchewan health planning commission, is quoted in the Toronto Star of February 5, 1950, as saying:
Since, as appears evident, Canada is approaching the day of decision concerning health insurance, the important question is, what kind of health insurance?
The editorial goes on:
Dr. Taylor has suggested that this would depend on the answers to the following, among other questions:
1.	Should it be a national scheme, on the British model, or should there be ten different schemes, evolved by the provinces?
2.	Should professional associations have administrative authority? Should government funds be turned over to a profession or an association for distribution to its own members?
3.	How shall health insurance be paid for? Should it be entirely or partly financed by the state? Should it be compulsory or voluntary? Which of the three levels of government should participate and in what proportion? Should individuals pay according to a flat rate or by graded income tax levy? Should employers contribute?
4.	Should all services be provided from the start? If not, what should be included and what left out?
Now, it is quite true that the opposition will say that a committee is merely a stall,
IMr. Croll.]
but because that charge is made is no reason to refuse to set up a committee. With this government the public does not demand every promise in writing and notarized. They have given us their trust and confidence for almost two generations. We have not failed them. We, who have given this country every worthwhile social measure, intend to secure for the people whatever is required against the ravages of disease and ill health.
I have already indicated that there are many problems that need study. There are five particular aspects that have to be studied by some committee at some time. First is the question of health grants; what has been done with them and how effective they have been. Second is the question of provincial co-operation and how we can obtain it. Third are the voluntary agencies and how we can integrate them. Fourth is the attitude of the medical profession, how we can pacify them. Fifth is the question of costs and their distribution.
I think, in the light of these problems, it is clear that only a committee could now make progress to blueprint a health insurance program. We need to assess our manpower, facilities, knowledge, and funds to be used for health insurance. It is true that the time is short. It is not likely that any committee could be organized before the middle of January. If there should be a spring election it would be almost impossible for the committee to complete its deliberations. If, on the other hand, there should be an election in the fall it may be possible to bring in a report before we adjourn, which would be about the middle of May. I do not know, but I believe it is time we got at the job.
I have said that a committee could recommend a formula for health insurance, but it would do more than that. It would help prepare the country for health insurance and perhaps deal with the most pertinent problem before us: shall it be all or nothing at this time? In its wisdom it may well recommend a limited service to be increased progressively; that has been the experience with every plan that is in existence at the present time. It is quite possible the committee may find that the country is in a position to undertake immediately or within the very near future hospitalization or diagnostic treatment. The medical profession generally welcome the extension of hospitalization to the public, and I think they would co-operate fully. Perhaps that would be our first step. I am sure none of us is prepared to accept a half-baked plan that may well set back health insurance for a generation in this country.
When I said that health insurance ranks high on the government's list of unfinished

business I heard someone across the floor say "hear, hear." I believe it would be worth while, in the few minutes I have at my disposal, to look at the position of the other political parties in the house on health insurance. Their position is put forward in Hansard. The position of the official opposition is found at page 29 of Hansard for November 24:
For that reason there should be general agreement that the first and necessary step in dealing with this subject is to institute an inquiry which would be conducted by representatives of the medical profession, the hospital boards, the dominion, provincial and municipal governments.
The position of the Social Credit party is found at page 56 of Hansard for November 24:
The Social Credit kind of national health program 'would ensure that sufficient doctors, dentists, nurses, technicians, clinics and hospital beds would be made available first to take on the work as the scheme is extended.
In so far as the C.C.F. position is concerned, they say: "Health insurance here and now; we have had enough committees and surveys. What we want now is action." It is obvious from the statements on the record, and we who are parliamentarians know exactly what all the parties mean. We can reach only one conclusion. The Liberal party is the only party that can bring health insurance to the Canadian people because the Tories won't and the C.C.F. can't.

speechtext: My suggestion is that this is the time to begin. If we do not, we shall be answerable to future generations for our complacency and our failure. So long as a single life is lost unnecessarily; so long as one person endures suffering which could have been prevented; so long as sickness takes its needless toll, then we shall have failed in our responsibility to the Canadian people. I repeat my suggestion that at this time we can make progress in one way and one way only, by setting up a committee of this house or a joint committee to blueprint health insurance.
