speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon 1 wish to direct some attention to the Canadian beet sugar industry as it relates to national defence. There are in Canada at present seven beet sugar facories. There are three in Alberta, all in *'he Lethbridge area, one in Manitoba and two in Ontario, as well as one in Quebec. These seven factories can produce an estimated 25 per cent of the needs of Canadians in respect of sugar. Both the sugar beet growers and the sugar beet factory owners are fearful that this valuable Canadian industry is in
The Address-Mr. Blackmore grave danger. It can be destroyed before long by the rising importations of Cuban granulated cane sugar.
The Chatham Daily News of November 7, 1952, carries the following headlines:
Sugar beet industry facing extinction.
Refined Cuban sugar floods domestic market.
By Ted Aitkin
In the lower right-hand corner of the front page appeared this headline:
Sugar beet marketing board urges Ottawa to protect sugar beet industry.
The same newspaper in its November 17 issue on page 11 carried this headline:
Cuban refined sugar forces down domestic beet payment.
As everybody knows, if domestic beet payments are forced down our farmers will be warned away from the production of sugar beets. Thus the industry could be easily destroyed.
Far too few Canadians realize how serious a situation this could indicate, first as regards Canadian sugar supply in case of war and even in peace, and second, as regards Canadian sovereignty.
Let me review some of the facts concerning the sugar supply in world war II. In Canada sugar rationing was introduced on July 1, 1942, and continued until November 3, 1947. Throughout most of this period the household ration was a half pound per person per week, plus a varying extra allowance during the home canning season. In 1945 the ration was reduced to about, six ounces a week. The industrial users of sugar such as bakers, confectioners, soft drink manufacturers, etc., were rationed at varying rates at varying times from as low as 50 per cent to as high as 90 per cent of the July, 1941, usage.
The total annual per capita consumption of sugar, direct and indirect, including the sugar content in jams, biscuits, confectionery, canned fruit, etc., is indicated in the first column below. The second column gives the total annual per capita consumption of sugar in all its forms, including the sugar content of glucose, corn syrup, honey, etc. The table is as follows:

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
By glancing at those figures we can readily see how seriously the people of Canada were limited in the matter of sugar consumption. Sugar is one of the absolute musts in the diet.
Let us see what were the main causes of this rationing, that we may be able to judge whether or not those causes can apply in any coming conflict in which Canada may be engaged.
First, there was a sharp reduction in the world output. The Philippine sugar industry was destroyed. The sugar industry of Java was destroyed. The sugar industry of many of the European nations, especially those that were occupied and overrun, was in large measure destroyed. Such countries as Poland and the Ukraine also had their sugar industry destroyed.
Production was greatly impaired in such countries as Australia, Fiji, Trinidad and Antigua. This impairment was caused by a variety of reasons. One would be lack of fertilizers, and there were many others.
The total falling off in the world's production of sugar amounted to 8 million tons. This falling off reduced the world sugar production from 31 million tons in 1939-40 to 23 million tons in 1945. These figures I take from a report of the wartime prices and trade board released in March of 1946.
Meanwhile the world population was increasing. We must make allowance for the rapid increase in the world population. Many people are afraid that we are not going to be able to produce all the food the world needs, even under the best of conditions. It is estimated that probably the world population is increasing at the rate of some 25 million a year, and that at this rate of increase the world population will practically double in the next 70 years. All those who are contemplating the production of food in the world should bear strictly in mind figures like that. Seventy years is not a long period. Babies lying in our cradles today will probably see that time and have to cope with the dreadful problems which will then prevail.
In any world war of at least the immediate future, we must expect still greater destruction of sugar production; for if matters continue as they are now we shall have Russia and her satellites, with a tremendous population, ranged against the United States and the so-called NATO and other free nations. That will mean that we shall have a world in conflict in two opposing camps, and all the rest of the world will be the battleground. There will not be much chance of producing 

sugar up to normal in most of the battleground and perhaps in much of the territory occupied and held by the great combatants.
Let it be borne in mind that we shall have submarines of far wider range, of far greater striking power and of much greater versatility in the next war than those we had in the last one; and submarines accounted for a good many cargoes of sugar. We shall also have aircraft of far greater range, striking power and versatility than those we had in the war just past. We shall have guided missiles, with all the fearful possibilities that could derive from their use in the matter of sinking cargoes of sugar that suppliers might attempt to bring to the Canadian shore. I am not mentioning the possibilities of the use of the atomic bomb and the hydrogen bomb. Just imagine what would be left of the finest of the sugar-producing islands if an atomic bomb or a hydrogen bomb were dropped on it. As sober Canadians in a responsible position we, together with the people throughout Canada, must take cognizance of these facts and must guide our future policies with our eyes upon those facts, not upon theories, no matter how much we might have loved those theories.
It will be argued that Canada might safely rely upon the United States to bolster the Canadian sugar supply in case of need. In world war II Canadians were fast wearing their welcome out as dependent neighbours of the United States in the matter of sugar supplies.
To bring this matter forcibly to the attention of all interested people throughout the country and throughout the house, I ask permission to read into Hansard a quotation from the United States Congressional Record of 1947, at page A507:
United States Press Criticizes Work of Sugar Pool. Extension of Remarks of Hon. Roy O. Woodruff of Michigan in The House of Representatives.
Thursday, January 30, 1947.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under leave granted to extend my remarks in the Record, I include the following article from Sugar Facts, published at Chatham, Ontario, of January 15, 1947:
United States Press criticizes work of sugar pool- Editorial comment supports Representative Woodruff's charge United States contributing more than fair share-Canada attacked as one giving less.
A letter forwarded to Hon. Thomas A. Jenkins, chairman of the Republican congressional food study committee, with respect to the sugar situation has occasioned a flood of editorial comment throughout the United States. Author of the letter, Representative Roy O. Woodruff (Republican), of Michigan, wrote in part: "With our beet-sugar production up and Cuba's production up, one may well ask why our sugar bowls are empty and why so much fruit and vegetables cannot be canned for lack of sugar. The answer is found in the program carried out by the combined food board,

which has lately been expanded into the international emergency food commission. The combined food board was composed of the United States, Great Britain and Canada. The United States and its offshore territories make the greatest contribution to the pool, as they furnish over 60 per cent of the sugar consumed in this country in addition to sharing with other nations the 3,768,000 tons which the United States bought from Cuba. In short, United States consumers get only 2,125,000 tons from Cuba, and the remaining 1,643,000 tons are distributed to other nations by the commission. By comparison, Britain will provide less than 30 per cent of her sugar consumption, whereas Canada will produce only 18 per cent of its sugar needs.
"Sugar rationing continues in the United States with promise of only a microscopic increase in allowances, yet Canada recently declared a sugar dividend of three extra pounds per person to her household consumers. This dividend has been reported in the press as being justified by increased supplies of sugar. Canada is producing only 65 per cent of its beet-sugar plant capacity, with the largest beet-sugar plant in Ontario standing idle for the past 5 years."
Mr. Woodruff's letter goes on to quote J. H. Blackmore, M.P., who told the Canadian House of Commons, "I am utterly amazed at the indifference which prevails in this house and in the Dominion of Canada with respect to the sugar supply."
"It is obvious," wrote Mr. Woodruff, "that the administration in Washington has simply stood on the sidelines and let the American producers and consumers carry the load for other nations".
The press of the United States sprang eagerly to Mr. Woodruff's cause. The Tri-County Banner, of Blanchard, Mich., ran his letter under a page 1 headline, "Bureaucrats cause of sugar shortage, claims Woodruff".
The Bay City Times editorialized "He deserves the gratitude of the public for starting the ball rolling." The Detroit Sunday Times, reporting a speech by James Vernor, ginger ale tycoon, headed the story, "United States sugar shortage laid to new deal plan." The same paper, in another story, reports "In Washington, stacks of letters from outraged housewives, denouncing the sugar shortage and demanding relief, are being exhibited by congressmen."
The Los Angeles Examiner ran a banner headline, "Housewives' sugar fight urged" with a page 1 box "Want more sweets? Tell Congressmen." The Detroit Times of December 24 cried plaintively, "Europe got (our) Yule sugar."
Senator Bridges, Republican, from New Hampshire, warned Secretary of Agriculture Anderson to supply sugar, declaring that while Anderson is prepared to ask only 9 pounds more sugar per person in 1947, sugar industry experts have produced figures showing that were Americans to get their rightful share they would have 19 pounds more sugar per person than in 1946.
The Detroit Free Press quoted Chairman Jenkins, of the Republican food study commission, as saying, "The American housewife has suffered more than her share of the wartime sugar shortage as compared with the industrial user of sugar . . . any increase in the ration for 1947 beyond the 20 per cent extra already recommended should go directly to individual housewives." (The 20 per cent increases suggested by Jenkins are double the amount of increase considered likely for 1947 by the department of agriculture.)
Anyone reading that statement will readily see that if the war had gone on for two or three more years those protests would have
The Address-Mr. Blackmore registered in congress with such vigour that congressmen would have been forced to take action and Canada would have been without the sugar we had, little as it was. I hope we shall all bear in mind, inside this house and outside the house, that very solemn fact.
It will be argued that there is a world surplus of sugar production. That is no responsibility of Canada or Canadians. It seems to me that I have known a good many people who feel that because there is a world surplus of sugar we ought to do something about it. We do not have to do anything about it. Let those who are overproducing do something about it. Every nation certainly has an inalienable right to increase its production of any commodity to the point of self-sufficiency in respect of that commodity, provided that the nation is. well adapted for the production of that commodity.
There can be no conceivable doubt that Canada is eminently fitted for the production of sugar. Canadians can produce all the sugar they need in the province of Alberta alone, south of High River. In my own constituency where there are now three sugar factories, there could be two more. I am not saying there should be, but there could be. We are now constructing the great St. Mary-Milk river water conservation project, which will put water on 350,000 odd acres. Thirty thousand acres, according to the estimates of those who know, will support a sugar factory of 1,500 tons slicing capacity such as is the factory at Raymond, in my constituency, which can supply Canadians with roughly 5 per cent of their sugar needs.
We also have the Canada Land and Irrigation project. We have the Eastern irrigation project around Brooks and Rosemary. These all comprise land which is eminently suitable for the production of sugar. These irrigation projects together with others in southern Alberta would provide land for the production of all the sugar needed by Canada's present population. There may be objection to subsidizing the price of the sugar, or the freight on it, so as to move it down to Ontario and Quebec or out to British Columbia where it may be needed. But the simple fact is we can physically produce the sugar.
In Ontario there is room for many sugar factories. In Saskatchewan, in the Carrot river valley, sugar can be produced with great success, according to estimates. Sugar is also being produced in Manitoba. We have no grounds for supposing that Manitoba could not support another sugar factory. Therefore there is simply no conceivable

The Address-Mr. Blackmore excuse lor Canada's failure to produce sufficient sugar to meet her needs, and to do so under highly economic conditions, as I shall show before I finish my remarks.
It will be argued that the beet sugar industry is an uneconomic industry, unable to compete successfully with the cane sugar industry without subsidies and various kinds of help, the whole result being that by using the beet sugar industry the way we do we are making our consumers pay an unjustly high cost for sugar. I propose to read into the record an excerpt from the submission to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations by the Alberta co-operative sugar beet growers association in 1937. From a perusal of this excerpt in this report it will be easy for anyone to see that the beet sugar industry can hold its own quite successfully if it is not subjected to handicaps to which no one in his right mind would think of subjecting any industry.
When you stop to think of the kind of protection which is given our manufacturing industries producing agricultural machines, our manufacturing industry producing automobiles, and almost every other industry including wheat, apples, carrots, table beets, cabbages, and almost anything you can name, when you consider the protection given these you begin to say: "Well, an ordinary amount of protection to the Canadian beet sugar industry is only logical." I read:
To indicate the value of this industry to the agriculture of our district, the community in general and the Dominion of Canada, we submit the following figures relating to the 1937 beet crop: 235,481 tons of beets were produced from 19,829 acres of irrigated land-an average of 11-88 tons per acre; 75,603,700 pounds of sugar were manufactured; 3,813 pounds was the per acre yield of refined sugar; $3,040,000 worth of sugar was manufactured; $155 was the total gross return per acre; $77.50 was the gross return to the manufacturer; $77.50 was the gross return per acre to the farmer.
The farmers' costs approximated $60 per acre which includes $25 per acre paid for hand labour by the farmer. Those figures were given in a speech made by T. George Wood, manager, Canadian Sugar Factories Limited at Lethbridge, Wednesday, March 23, 1938. We believe that this land is producing more food value per acre than any other land in the dominion.
I believe it was, too. I continue:
Sugar beets of the highest quality can be grown, harvested and manufactured into refined sugar on all of our irrigated lands in Alberta. This industry has, in the districts where it is established, made a tremendous contribution toward the prosperity of both the urban and rural sections and to our national economy.
The annual returns from the Lethbridge northern irrigation district rose from $761,000 in 1935 to $1,057,000 in 1936, the first year the new sugar factory operated in that territory.

The sugar factory referred to is the one at Picture Butte.
I continue:

The average for Alberta for the same years was 8 0 tons per acre. For the year 1937 the average yield in Alberta was 11-88 per acre, while in the United States it was 11-77. As for the quality of beets in Alberta, the average sugar content from 1925 to 1937 was 16-6 per cent, while for the 1937 crop it was 18-16 per cent.
I wish to state now, Mr. Speaker, that 18-16 per cent would probably be one of the very highest sugar content figures to be found on the American continent, and perhaps ini most countries of the world-.
Since 1937 the mechanization of the beet sugar industry has progressed- tremendously and spectacularly. Now it is possible, by the use of remarkable machinery which has been developed, to carry on almost any process in connection with the production of sugar beets almost entirely by machinery. I saw this year a number of machines being pulled along by tractors. There would be two people standing on the machine and operating it, carrying out the work of digging the beets, topping them, and dumping them into a truck being driven alongside. The machine would travel just a little faster than a team would pull a -plow. Well, that is enough to show that the beet sugar industry has a wonderful future before it. It is not a thing that ought to be kicked around.
Since 1946, Mr. Speaker, Liberal government policy has permitted an enormous increase in the -cost of production of beet sugar. Nevertheless sugar from sugar beets at present prices easily surpasses other staple foods in respect of comparative cost -per calorie. To support this assertion may I read into the record- a statement which is printed in the November 20, 1952 issue of Sugar Facts, which the United States congressman thought worthy of quoting. The quotation is as follows:
Sugar Is a Bargain In Our Food Budget
With the price of proteins-steaks and roasts- what it is today, Canadians have a cheap energy food in sugar. It is estimated that in Canada and

United States today, about one-fourth of the energy requirement is met through eating sugar in various forms at fire sale prices.
Scientists claim the average person uses approximately 3,000 calories per day and witness how cheaply sugar-compared to today's high prices for other foods-can supply the much needed energy.
If food is purchased on a caloric basis alone, and flavor and variety disregarded, the costs for 1,000 calories are:

Those figures seem to hew out from under them the ground upon which those men would stand who feel that we should import sugar from Cuba, because of the need to reduce sugar prices. I know that any Canadian government is likely to be under almost irresistible pressure demanding the admission of cheap cane sugar into Canada. Any Canadian government requires all the support possible to help resist such pressure.
The people of Canada, and some members of the House of Commons, will be interested to know that there are five agencies in the world today, several of them right here in Canada, that are seeking to destroy the Canadian beet sugar industry, for various reasons. First in Canada we have the owners of cane refineries. These men obviously would like to get rid of the beet sugar industry. Second, we have Canadians who have invested money in plantations in cane producing countries. There are some powerful men in both those classes. Third, there are the Canadian interests eager to sell abroad. It is easy enough, for example, for automobile or machinery manufacturers to say, "Well, bring in Cuban sugar. Let us have a chance to sell our goods abroad."
Fourth are the internationalists and world centralizers. No nation can be entirely free that is not able to produce its own needs of life. Now, there are men in the world-and if every member in the house does not know them, he ought to-who are seeking definitely to deprive nations of their sovereignty. Nothing could possibly be better designed to destroy Canada's sovereignty than to place her in a vulnerable position in respect of sugar. In case any government which internationalists might desire to control should
The Address-Mr. Blackmore be elected in Canada, the internationalist would say, "Now, look, you government of Canada, if you put your foot on the dotted line, you will get your sugar. But if you do not, we are not so sure about it."
That may sound grotesque; nevertheless it is real. If we do not recognize that fact and govern ourselves accordingly, our children and our children's children will suffer because of our neglect.
The fifth group are the doctrinaire unrealists enamoured of fallacious philosophies of international trade. There exists in Canada the widest diversity of opinion in respect of international trade. We have heard these opinions expressed right here on the floor of the house. We have heard extremes on both sides. Probably the extremes are wrong; but it is a very easy matter to make serious mistakes in respect of international trade and its over-all necessity and desirability. I am now making no comment on the matter, more than to say that every man in Canada and every woman in Canada will do well to review with the utmost care his philosophy of international trade, to see whether or not he or she has been making a mistake.
I have spoken this afternoon to help strengthen the hand of each minister striving to protect the Canadian beet sugar industry. I know in the present Canadian cabinet there are many ministers who realize the value of the beet sugar industry and who desire to protect it. But there are also men in the cabinet, I fear, who do not realize the value of the beet sugar industry and who do not want to protect it. I have spoken of those who desire to protect it, and I would venture the assumption that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is among those who so desire.
At a later time I shall have something to say about other aspects of the Canadian beet sugar industry. But I submit that anyone who takes into consideration the arguments I have presented this afternoon will realize with me that it is a policy bordering on absolute lunacy to permit enough cane sugar to come into Canada, to seriously impair or possibly destroy the beet sugar industry of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the gift of oratory is a great gift, but it should never be dilapidated in such a way as to obscure true facts or issues. When we in this house were privileged to listen to the ear-flattering utterances of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Drew), I am sure that I and other hon. members were inspired with greater reverence for the Creator of all things who with His usual wisdom in His munificence gives to those to whom He denies forensic ability the compensation of an added measure of patience so that we may bear with sound in order that eventually we may hope truth and fact will emerge.
On the second day of this session it was with no small degree of humility and with still more patience that we on this side listened to the opening oration of the Leader of the Opposition in the hope that this year he might say what he has never said; that he might at last firmly establish his position


or his right to the potential leadership of this country. But as usual it was a forlorn hope.
When on November 24 the Leader of the Opposition went ferreting out facts and figures in the field of defence expenditures we who were here in 1949 were reminded of his ill-fated adventure in a similar field. I am sure that no one living in or about Montreal will ever forget the extraordinary statements about Canadair made by the hon. gentleman nor his no less extraordinary mishap following those accusations. That memory will condition the reception in Montreal and Quebec and throughout Canada of the latest of these sorties by the Leader of the Opposition.
I think he should be aware by now that a keen mind for haberdashery is not necessarily a criterion of great political sagacity. While his detailing of military ties, raincoats, shoes, etc. was most interesting, I am sure, to one whose mind has a bent for trivia, it could hardly be taken by this country as evidence of leadership. I fear that as usual the Progressive Conservative party in its quest for what we call in French "la petite bete" has by-passed the main issue, which is good government and leadership. The attitude of the Leader of the Opposition is somewhat akin to that of a concert conductor who forgets the general conducting of a concerto in a search for fly specks among his notes.
There may be fly specks on the defence inventory ledgers in the form of overstocking of boots, ties, forks, knives and overcoats, but they are only fly specks. Before any hon. member on the other side accuses me of considering hundreds and thousands and millions of dollars as being fly specks, let me say to hon. members that I have an honest regard and a great fondness for the dollar, and I have a very especial regard for the public dollar.
I do not consider that the unnecessary expenditure of dollars can be characterized as fly specks, but I would remind the house that the hon. gentleman has not accused this government of throwing away money. He has simply accused the government of having overstocked or stocked in excess certain of these supplies which are necessary for our present or eventual defence.
As I say, these may be fly specks in our defence ledgers, but that is not too surprising to anyone who has been connected with big business in private enterprise. In spite of all precautions to protect one's own interest, it is frequently found that ill-advised and perhaps unnecessary commitments are made. Expenditures or purchases may be entered into because of confidence in firms or individuals which may from time to time be

misplaced. But such incidents are not deprecated in private industry unless they are so serious as to compromise the success of the over-all operation. They are treated in their proper light as a minor incident in the general scheme of the operation.
If every private business were to be scrutinized by the Leader of the Opposition in the same way few if any would come out unscathed, few if any of those whom we consider our business leaders would escape. That would sound the death knell of private enterprise. The hon. gentleman would do better, I think, to concentrate his mind on the over-all picture. He would do better to bring to this house a different viewpoint, a viewpoint more appropriate to this house and I would suggest that he would do much better to leave the searching of fly specks to one or two others who have delegated unto themselves the authority for such searching. The attitude of those gentlemen, I might remind him, toward private enterprise, qualifies them much better to pass impartially on both private and public expenditures.
The hon. gentleman is absent now because of other inevitable commitments, but no doubt he is familiar with something which is along the line of what he, in public affairs recently, has been discussing. I read a headline from the Montreal Herald of Friday, November 28: "Gang rooks oil company for $3 million". The story inside goes on to say that one oil company in Montreal through the dishonesty of its subalterns was rooked of $3 million. The hon. gentleman will also recall the unfortunate incident which happened to one of our leading banks not very long ago. He would be inclined to agree with me, I am sure, that these things happen in private business; and they are relegated to their proper position in private business as they should be in public affairs. I am sure that none of the heads of either business will be accused or will be found guilty if they are accused of having mismanaged or misdirected the affairs which were entrusted to them.
During a speech on November 24 the hon. gentleman took it upon himself to deal with television. I do not intend to dissect here his speech on television. There will be many other opportunities and may I convey to him, and ask his followers to convey to him, the statement that I shall welcome every single opportunity. The hon. gentleman stated, as appears in Hansard of November 24, page 24, when dealing with television:
This is strangely inconsistent with the decision made just two weeks ago by the government of the United Kingdom which still retains a monopoly . . .
Mr. Speaker, it may be strangely inconsistent to the Leader of the Opposition that
The Address-Mr. Beaudry we in this country are determined to lead Canadian affairs with some degree of inconsistency with other countries, perhaps. However, the statement by the hon. gentleman is far from being inconsistent with Conservative policy. It is not inconsistent with the manner in which too many of them too long have thought too little of self-operation in Canada. I would suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that when we do resume discussion of radio and television broadcasting he bring to this house a slightly different approach, determined in his mind that discussion is going to be allowed on the basis of Canadian things for Canada and Canada for Canadian people, not on the basis of whether our manner of conducting Canadian affairs is consistent or inconsistent with the operation of-let us call them by name-Tory governments of other countries.

I heard that four years ago from exactly the same source.
May I now deal with another of the gentlemen who sit on that side of the house, the member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche). On November 25 he established just how firmly he believes in Voltaire's theory "Mentez, mentez, il en restera toujours quelque chose". I refer to page 73 of Hansard for November 25 where amongst other things he says:
Radio-Canada peut imposer ses programmes aux postes prives. Radio-Canada exige un permis one-reux de chaque transmetteur de postes prives...
The translation reads:
The C.B.C. can impose its own programs on private stations. Private stations are compelled to pay costly licence fees to the C.B.C. for each of their transmitters, and the C.B.C. uses those revenues to build stations of its own that will compete with private enterprise.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the hon. gentleman refers to television and radio with the contempt which can be brought only by his obvious lack of familiarity with the situation. I would say to him if he were here, and I will say to him when he and I again discuss television, that although I may not speak with the same assurance I speak with a modicum of authority. For the benefit of those gentlemen on the other side of the house who may not be aware of it, for some years I owned, operated and managed the only private network of radio stations then existing. In order to allay any possibility that hon. gentlemen might put their foot in it and accuse anyone of political favouritism, let me state that I purchased that private radio network as an operating network. The people from whom I purchased it were then known and are still

The Address-Mr. Beaudry known, notably in one case, as recognizing politically only one liege lord, the present Leader of the Opposition.
May I say to the hon. gentleman that when one comes to this house he is not perhaps expected to be fully familiar with all that has been placed on our statute books over a period of years; but surely when discussing matters with such authority and assurance as the hon. gentleman did, and when discussing a question which the Conservative party is determined to place in an exalted position this year, the hon. gentleman should at least become cognizant of the relevant act. The hon. gentleman has stated that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation can impose its programs upon private radio stations, but there he is so far away from the truth that one wonders if he should be accused of gross ignorance or perhaps of wandering away from the truth by habit. If the hon. gentleman has a copy of the act I would suggest that at the first opportunity, which will be either tonight or tomorrow, he quote me one line or one word from the act which authorizes him to state that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation .... "peut imposer ses programmes aux postes prives" .... can impose its programs on private radio stations.
There is, however, one reference in section 8. The corporation may for that purpose:
(d) make operating agreements with private stations for the broadcasting of programs.
If, of course, his contention stems from the general inference that parliament can do anything then of course he is right-but only if his assertion stems from that inference-and even then perhaps he should be reminded that the inference is valueless in this discussion. It is an admitted legal principle that the only thing parliament cannot do, at least this was the example given when I attended legal schools, is to change a man into a woman. But, I understand, in at least two countries recently that has been done, so perhaps the maxim should be changed. I would suggest to the professors of law-at least in that part of the country where I live, because as you all know we have a different code of law than the rest of the country-that the simile be changed and that we now quote as an instance of the power of parliament, "The only thing parliament cannot do is to change the present crop of Conservatives into statesmen."
The hon. member having established to his own satisfaction and perhaps to no one else's that the C.B.C. can impose its programs on private radio stations-which is not true-he goes on to say that the C.B.C. yearly charges onerous fees to the private radio stations in order that it may set up stations of its own


to compete with private enterprise. The hon. member for Labelle, I am afraid, uses the word "onerous" as one of the imponderable words with which he is not too familiar, and which could mean anything to him. In order to help him mathematically, if he can follow me, I shall point out to him that last year the entire revenue received by the Department of Transport to be turned over to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the entire revenue collected from some 120 private radio stations in this country, amounted to $221,000. I think a simple process of very elementary division will bring us to the conclusion that the radio stations in this country operating privately paid, on the average, a sum of $1,800 a year for this privilege.
I may say this to the hon. member for Labelle before he leaves us permanently, which I am reasonably sure will be within a matter of months. Does he know why this money is collected from private radio stations? Does he know to what use that money is being put. In his own words, the fee is exacted so that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation may extend its network of national stations in order the better to compete with private radio. I do not believe the hon. member is aware of the original purpose of this fee. Until a few years ago this fee was not payable to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation but to the Department of Transport and was used to meet part of the expenses, not for national radio but for the upkeep of private radio; for the monitoring of private radio; for the reading of schedules of private radio, and all those things which are necessary if this country is going to supervise, as does every other country, the operations of private radio.
May I also ask the hon. gentleman this? Does he know why this money, formerly handled by the Department of Transport, is being turned over to the C.B.C.? If he does not, let me ask him one other question? Does he know that his own compatriots, the Frenchspeaking Canadians in northern Quebec, only have radio because the C.B.C. has helped them to get it? Does he know, or is that inconsistent with the higher feelings of his party, that a group of French-speaking Canadians in northern Ontario is entirely dependent upon the C.B.C. and its association with private stations? Does he know that that is true of another segment of northern Ontario; or is he aloof to that? Does he know that a large part of those fees collected now go towards giving the French-speaking people of St. Boniface, in the province of

Manitoba, radio programs which they could not have without the C.B.C.? Is it unimportant in his eyes, sitting on that side of the house, that the payment of these fees also means that a French-language group on the fringe of Edmonton and in the south of Alberta are provided with radio in their own tongue? That is our concept of national radio. This is made possible because the C.B.C., despite the hon. member for Labelle and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Drew), collects from each of 120 private radio stations an average of $1,800 a year.
Much has been said, Mr. Speaker, on the subject of radio and television. I repeat that there will be other opportunities to discuss these questions, and I repeat that I shall welcome every single one of them. As usual, consistent with the true philosophy and true mores of the Progressive Conservative party, they believe that in everything the principle should be by-passed for the exception, the truth for the half truth or even a lesser part. I feel sorry for the hon. member for Labelle. I feel sorry because he failed to bring with him into this house the only sword with which he should have girded his loins, the sword of truth. He preferred to fill his scabbard with split hairs in the hope that one would be suddenly transmuted into a weapon which he could wield in defence of private radio.
I have taken more time than I intended, Mr. Speaker, but may I conclude with this. From time to time I have meetings with a friend of mine, an ancient Asiatic philosopher who deigns to impart to this undeserving one some of his Chinese philosophy. May I commend to the Leader of the Opposition and his party this fable, divested of its native garb and shorn of its oriental embellishments. "Time is like all commodities, cheap to him who has it in abundance but so precious to him who uses it to the hilt. The wise man, wishing to determine whether it is day or night, is content with looking at the sun; but the foolish man would rather ignore the sun the better to watch the sweep hand of the clock." In this country most of us are content to be guided by the sun. The clock watching, the sweep hand watching of the Conservative party, can only earn its leader and itself one lone degree. I take a great deal of pleasure in conferring upon the Leader of the Opposition and his party a degree-given I am sure with the best wishes of the majority of this house who join in the accolade to the leader of the Conservative party, who has earned it during the last three years in this house and by his opening speech on November 24-the degree of master of trivia. In view of his exalted position, I should add summa cum ignominia.

speechtext:
should like to add my congratulations to those of the previous speakers to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the

The Address-Mr. Charlton speech from the throne. I should also like to congratulate the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) on being elevated to cabinet positions. I do not mean to refer to the speech of the hon. member who spoke just previous to the dinner hour other than to say it is rather unfortunate that the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Beaudry) does not visit us more often.
The throne speech unfortunately offers nothing to eastern farmers. Since becoming a member of this House of Commons I have tried to impress upon the government the importance of agriculture to the nation. Everything which detracts from the economic position of the farmer must eventually reflect on the national economy. The effect that is being felt now in industry and in urban municipalities is obvious from several quarters. The income of the average 100-acre farm will be reduced this year by approximately $1,000. In other words every farmer has taken a $1,000 cut in wages, or approximately $20 a week. In spite of that fact, the prices of the products the farmer has to buy have gone up. Can you imagine the howl that would be put up in this House of Commons if we as members were asked to take a reduction of $1,000 in our indemnities? Farmers in general, but particularly those adjacent to urban municipalities, are being taxed off their farms. Land alone should not be expected to bear such a high proportion of the taxation burden. There must be some incentive at least to keep people who are on the land at the present time interested, if we want food.
The farmers' buying power is an important factor in any community. That buying power has been reduced by a considerable amount this year, and farmers are wondering just what the future holds for them. They are becoming more cost-conscious every year, and are dropping the non-paying branches of the industry. There are those who wonder whether the dairy cow is headed for oblivion, just as the work horse is an historic monument of the past.
We cannot expect any industry in this country to survive if it is forced to compete with the cheaper labour of another land. This government is forcing two of the greatest industries in this country out of business through an apparent lack of interest in their problems. I refer to the textile and dairy industries and I mention them jointly because they are faced with an identical problem, that of unbearable competition from lower wage-rate countries.
We are fighting a desperate and costly battle against communism which we call a

cold war. Our most devastating weapon in this fight is truth. With it we can build the strength of the democratic nations and undermine that of our enemies. We in the opposition are seeking the truth. The government hedges, and hedging is the mother of suspicion, and distrust. The Canadian people are carrying a terrific burden of overtaxation. They are ready and willing to pay their fair share, and know that defence expenditures are necessary in these troubled times. But are we getting value for our money?
We as individuals are forced to cut our costs and increase the efficiency of our operations. Why can't the government? People ask me why the Department of National Defence bought ten pairs of shoes per man, when most of us are lucky if we have two pairs, or why it is necessary to have 12 neckties per man and three serving forks for every five men in the service. If a housewife ever bought for her family in the same proportion little Jimmy would have to do without shirts to pay for the neckties, and the Sunday roast would have to be cancelled to pay for the forks to serve it.
I am sure everyone in this country, especially the government, was glad to see the recent announcement in the press regarding the lifting of the United States embargo on livestock and hay. During the past nine months the meat packers of this country have enjoyed the proverbial Roman holiday. I commend the government for the idea of floor prices on beef and pork, but I must criticize them severely for the administration of that policy. Suggested prices to producers have certainly not been maintained on the lower grades, and. prices to consumers on the same grades have not dropped by anywhere near the same proportions. In other words the producer has been left at the mercy of the packer, and the consumer has not received the benefit.
Another serious problem for farmers today is the livestock feed situation. While the western producer naturally wants to get a fair price for his grain, the eastern feeder can afford to pay only a price that will give a fair return when, the finished product is marketed. On previous occasions in this house I have given the spread between the western producer and the eastern feeder. I was disappointed this afternoon when the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) was speaking. I thought he was going to delve further into that matter, but apparently he did not want to. According to an article in the Canadian Federation of Agriculture news

information bulletin of October, 1952, Dr. E. C. Hope, economist for that organization, reveals the spread on No. 1 feed oats at 38-3 cents a bushel, or $1.13 a hundredweight, and on No. 1 feed barley, 52-6 cents a bushel, or $1.09 a hundredweight. If the government, through its wheat board, cannot find some solution to this problem, then it should step aside and let farmer organizations handle the problem of feed grain between western producer and eastern feeder without any strings attached to it.
The government, finally realizing the importance of our water resources, is considering some measures of conservation. I take a great pride, Mr. Speaker, in the fact that those along the Grand river have been the first to pioneer water conservation and flood control. The organization now known as the Grand valley conservation authority is to be congratulated on its accomplishments, and I sincerely hope that this government will contribute their share toward the Conestogo project which was passed upon and accepted by the provincial government some time ago.
I have said on several occasions in this house that, rural mail carriers have been grossly underpaid. The government has finally decided to do something to correct this injustice, but I will withhold further comment until it is known what the proposal is.
I am sure all hon. members have received the memorandum prepared jointly by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and the Canadian Council of the Blind with reference to the elimination of the means test in the Blind Persons Act of Canada. I support that request, and I most sincerely hope the government will this session bring down the required legislation to eliminate this embarrassing means test.	,
The throne speech mentions a bill which will be introduced to place the historic sites and monuments board of Canada on a statutory basis. We in Brant are very proud of our forefathers and the part they played in the development of our country. The triennial conference of the Associated Countrywomen of the World with a membership of six million in 25 different countries will meet in Toronto in August, 1953. The chief aim of this organization is to improve rural conditions in all parts of the world. This conference has a special significance to members of the women's institutes in the riding which I represent. Last June when we allotted money to this association in our government estimates I made mention of this fact. It was in this district that Adelaide Hunter Hoodless, founder of the now world-wide
The Address-Mr. Charlton organization, was born and attended public school. The white frame house, her birthplace, still stands in our community. Little did anyone dream that this child would be the founder of an organization which has done so much for rural women and their respective communities.
We also had the distinction of having a cairn marking Mrs. Hoodless' birthplace erected in the district and unveiled by Lady Tweedsmuir in 1937. It is situated in a small park at the junction of highways 5 and 24. Funds for its erection were raised by the women's institutes of Brant county. In the 1947-49 Tweedsmuir historical competition, St. George won first place in Ontario. In 1949-51 competition, Glen Morris won first in Ontario and second in the dominion competition. As a matter of fact, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) were present in 1950 when an oil painting of Mrs. Hoodless, presented to Canada by the federated women's institutes of Ontario, was unveiled and hung in the archives by Mrs. Raymond Sayre from the United States, then president of the Associated Countrywomen of the World.
In view of the fact that the conference of the Associated Countrywomen of the World is to be held in Toronto next year, and delegates from many countries will be visiting this cairn and the birthplace of Mrs. Hoodless, I would sincerely hope that the historic sites and monuments board would see fit to suitably mark this cairn before the date of the conference.
On several previous occasions I have asked the government, through the historic sites and monuments board, to aid in some suitable way the council of the Six Nations reservation in the restoration and preservation of Chiefs-wood, birthplace of Pauline Johnson, well-known and gifted Indian poetess. Chiefswood was built over one hundred years ago, and if restored could be made into one of the greatest tourist attractions along the Grand river. Many distinguished visitors from England, Europe and America have been entertained there by Chief Johnson and his English bride, Emily Howells. From Chiefswood, Pauline Johnson became a national figure and her memory will ever remain in the hearts of those who knew her.
I also mentioned on previous occasions the Mohawk chapel, properly known as St. Paul's, His Majesty's Chapel of the Mohawks. This little church was built in 1780 for the Mohawk people who emigrated from New York to Canada during the war of independence, and is the oldest Protestant church in Upper Canada. Contained in this church is a stained leather bible and a silver communion set,

The Address-Mr. Jones both gifts of Queen Anne of England to the Mohawks, and carried by them during the war of independence from the old church at Fort Hunter in New York to be buried under a tree more than five years and borne north into safety at the conclusion of the war. Behind the altar in letters of gold are written the apostles' creed, the ten commandments and the Lord's prayer, all in the Indian language. To the left of the altar is one of the finest coats of arms in Canada, carved from a single block of oak and presented to the Indians by King George III.
I would be very remiss if I did not mention also the West Dumfries chapel built in 1845, commonly known as the Paris Plains church. For many years this old historic spot was not in use, but in 1948 interested citizens formed the Paris Plains restoration committee and have had the building restored as a memorial to the early pioneers of the district. Each year on the second Sunday in June a memorial outdoor church service is held.
I urge again the importance of restoring and marking such historic landmarks so they may stand as memorials to be seen and revered by future generations.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that when a member of this house recommends that consideration be given to certain necessary action, this involves the expenditure of public money. The expenditure of public money is made possible by taxation. Taxation in this country is at an unwarranted high level at present and should be reduced.
I sincerely believe, Mr. Speaker, that a firm determination by those in authority to eradicate waste and extravagance in governmental administration would not only make possible many essential services, but allow as well for necessary tax reductions in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment to the amendment moved by the C.C.F. Before doing so, however, there are one or two other comments I should like to make.
According to an answer given to a question asked in the house this week it would appear that at last the government has consented to purchase apple juice for the armed services. This is most gratifying to the processors of that excellent product, who have worked so hard in its production. It will also help the growers to recover some income from fruit that would be lost unless processed. I am pleased personally because nearly a year ago I brought to the attention of the house the fact that only imported juices were consumed by the armed forces, and that apple juice was excluded completely.
[Mr. Charlton.1

While this matter has reached a satisfactory conclusion, the fruit and vegetable growers of interior British Columbia still have several problems I should like to bring to the attention of the house. Tonight I shall deal briefly with only one of them, and that is the unfair competition offered by United States soft fruits and vegetables in our domestic market.
This situation is present across Canada, but it is particularly vicious in British Columbia. The extent of this market loss can be gauged by an article which appeared in Country Life, which is a monthly publication issued to the farmers of British Columbia and to my mind is one of the best dealing with farm and vegetable production in the Dominion of Canada. I take this publication as an authority on what they have to say about this particular market which has been lost.
The article reads:
It is hard to understand in a province capable of growing the widest diversity of the finest fruits and vegetables we yet continue to consume annually $3 million worth of vegetables imported from another country while only eating $2 million worth of our own B.C. grown vegetables. This would not be so if consumers knew of the relative nutritional values. It is an incongruous situation with some wholesalers importing foreign vegetables for your table at a time when the same produce grown in British Columbia is available. This can only be corrected by you, the consumer. When buying fresh vegetables insist on B.C. produce only.
If that condition exists generally across Canada it will mean a market loss running into many millions of dollars for our domestically produced vegetables and soft fruits. I agree to a certain extent with the article when it says that consumers can help, but the remedy is not there. The remedy must be brought about by government action.
This year soft fruits and vegetables were left on the trees and on the ground of the Okanagan valley because of a lack of markets. This applied particularly to prunes, peaches, and cabbages and other vegetables. I know of one veteran who was rather proud of an acre of cabbages which he had grown, but he was not able to sell a single cabbage on the market because it was filled already with cabbages that had been brought in from across the line. One grower went to Yakima to find out what the trouble was and he spoke to me on his return. He went to a packing house there where they were putting up tomatoes. Apparently the system has been changed in the United States because they now have a No. 1 grade and a No. 2 grade of tomatoes. This grower examined both grades and could not find one shade of difference. No. 1 was selling at $110 per ton and was practically all sold on the United States domestic market. No. 2 was listed at $55 per ton, but this grade was mostly in

storage. He inquired who purchased the No. 2 and he was told that although one or two cars had been sent to Seattle, the bulk was sent to the Canadian market.
It is true that they are offered for sale in small quantities, but probably the dealers in the United States are told, "we have none left." However, he was told that one or two cars had been sent to Seattle. This would conform with the dumping regulations which requires that they must be offered for sale in the country of origin at the price they are offered in Canada. In this case the price was one-half the price being asked for the No. 1 tomatoes and, as I pointed out, there was no discernible difference in the two grades.
The difficulty we are faced with is that our earliest crop comes on the market when the second or a later United States crop is also coming on the market. This is usually more plentiful and available at lower prices. This is a rather serious difficulty because there are many veterans who are going in for fruit growing who will have to wait five, six or eight years until their fruit trees are bearing. In the meantime they are trying to earn a livelihood by growing vegetables between the trees. They are being victimized because of these importations of competitive vegetables from the United States. For their sake and for the sake of other soft fruit and vegetable growers I ask the Department of Agriculture to investigate the situation.
I have not time to go into the details, but I do suggest that the situation be investigated at once and that steps be taken to protect our domestic market especially during the period when the market can be well and amply supplied by home-grown fruits and vegetables. A situation such as that described by Country Life, where the British Columbia market of $5 million is being shared on the basis of the domestic producer getting $2 million of it while our competitive neighbours to the south capture $3 million, is not healthy. That is why I appeal to the government for an early investigation with a view to taking steps to correct the situation before next year. There will be plenty of time, and I would be willing to give evidence as to what I claim is unfair competition brought about by the heavier crops produced in the United States.
I should like to deal now with the subject matter of our subamendment. Previous speakers, particularly Liberal speakers, have emphasized that before a national health plan can be entertained a good deal of ground work will have to be done, and they claim that this ground work is being done. Possibly part of that claim is correct, but I do
The Address-Mr. Jones feel that there is a branch of ground work that has been neglected, and I should like to deal briefly with it tonight.
One of the problems facing the Canadian people which the C.C.F. believes can be met successfully by the introduction of health insurance is a serious shortage of doctors, dentists, nurses and other health personnel as well as a shortage of hospitals and hospital facilities. My colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has dealt with the question of hospital shortages and some of the aspects of the nursing shortage, but I should like to deal particularly with the question of doctors and dentists.
By an authoritative standard, Canada is extremely short of doctors and the shortage of dentists is alarming. Furthermore the shortage is getting worse rather than better. The health grants program was designed primarily to overcome these shortages, but it has made almost no attempt to deal with the shortages in the fields that I have mentioned. According to an authoritative United States study which has been widely accepted in this country there should be one physician for every 704 persons. On this basis we should have had in Canada in 1951 a total of 19,904 physicians for our population of 14,009,429, whereas we had only 14,325 physicians. There was a shortage in that census year of 5,579 physicians in our country. If Canada is to reach an acceptable standard there must be an increase of more than 50 per cent in the number of doctors in this country.
What is actually happening? The situation since the end of the war has been getting worse rather than better. The population has been growing at a faster rate than the number of doctors. Thus in 1947 there was one active physician for every 938 people, but by 1951 the population per physician had gone up to 978.
The same alarming trend is noted with respect to dentists. There has been some increase in the number of dentists since the end of the war, but it has not nearly kept pace with the increase in population. In 1947 there was one dentist for every 2,729 people in Canada. In 1951 there was only one dentist for every 3,040 people. Thus the shortage of dentists in relation to the population has grown worse by more than 10 per cent in the four-year period. This deterioration in the supply of dentists in relation to the population is even more striking when it is examined in the light of acceptable standards. In 1943 there was one dentist for every 669 people in Canada's armed forces. If it is assumed that the civilian population should have at least as good care as was provided for members of the armed services this would have meant, on the basis of the

The Address-Mr. Jones 1951 population, a total of 20,940 dentists; but we actually had in that year only 4,608 dentists. Thus, the shortage of dentists in 1951 was 16,332. To reach the standard I have referred to would require almost a 400 per cent increase in the number of dentists.
This general shortage of doctors and dentists screens the fact, however, that the actual shortage in many of the more remote areas is far more acute and that a much higher percentage of doctors, dentists, and medical specialists is concentrated in the large cities. In 1949, 71-2 per cent of all physicians in Canada were located in urban centres of 10,000 and more population, but only 45-7 per cent of Canada's people resided in these cities. On December 1, 1946, 72 per cent of the dentists were located in urban centres of 10,000 population or more.
The reason for this maldistribution is not hard to And. Practice in the smaller centres is not so convenient as it is in the city. Facilities are inadequate. The income is lower and the social and cultural life is less attractive. But it is quite clear that if medical and dental training were made more readily available, if the hospital and research facilities were improved in rural areas, as they would be if a nation-wide health services plan were set up, many more young doctors would be attracted to service in rural areas.
We cannot overcome the shortages of dentists and doctors with our present facilities. There are only ten schools in Canada which offer complete medical courses and these are constantly overcrowded. We boast only five dental colleges. Clearly the training facilities have to be expanded, and this will mean federal financial assistance. Furthermore, it is a well known fact that the tuition fees at medical colleges and dental schools are very high. They are beyond the reach of the average Canadian student or his family. In 1946 the Canadian association of medical students and internes conducted a survey of the financial background of medical students. They found that the largest percentage of medical students came from the families which had the highest incomes; 28-6 per cent came from professional families but these families represented only 4-7 per cent of the total population. Only 12-2 per cent of the medical students came from Canada's farms where 36-5 per cent of the total population live. This survey further revealed that 7 [DOT] 3 per cent of the students polled were going through medical college entirely on their own resources. Three-quarters of them, 74-5 per cent, relied on their families as well as their own earnings, and 17-5 per cent were going through entirely at their families' expense. Nearly half were required to pay back their families after graduation.


Add to these economic difficulties the fact that medical school fees have more than doubled since 1925. In that year the average annual fee was $185; in 1945 it was $317; and in 1951 it was about $438. Dental college fees have climbed from approximately $293 in 1945 to about $385 in 1951. These fees are over and above what it costs the students to live during their courses and what it costs them for clothing and other expenses. The need for expanded training facilities and for a system of medical scholarships is selfevident. Not only is there a need for federal scholarships and bursaries for medical and dental students, but there is a need for special assistance to students who will undertake to practise in rural areas for a given number of years following graduation.
As I have said, the inauguration of health insurance itself, in addition to the particular measures I have just indicated, will do a great deal toward overcoming these shortages of personnel. This is made very clear in the Saskatchewan health survey report, "The Expanding Hospital System."
The continuing development of the hospitals of the province, with emphasis on district and regional as well as on the base hospitals, should have some influence in attracting physicians to areas outside the large urban centres. By placing emphasis on larger district hospitals, a number of advantages are obtained. The larger hospital can be more adequately equipped, it is better able to hold qualified technical and nursing personnel, and, with sufficient beds for more than one doctor, it helps to overcome the feeling of professional isolation. All of these factors operate to provide a better medical service for patients. As the national conference on rural health of the American Medical Association reported: "We do not want poor medical service made more available. Convenience is of secondary importance."
That the extension of the principle of prepayment has a favourable influence on the number and distribution of physicians has been shown by the experience of the municipal doctor plans and by the Swift Current medical care program.
Thus it will be seen that Saskatchewan's progress in hospital and health insurance is helping that province to overcome its very serious shortage of medical personnel. In one field, that of mental health, Saskatchewan has received rare praise. The world famous psychiatrist, Dr. Carl Menninger of the Men-ninger clinic, Topeka, Kansas, stated on September 20, 1951, a little over a year ago, that Saskatchewan was "the only area in the world that has all the competent psychiatrists it needs." He said that the psychiatric aid training program being carried out in Saskatchewan was the envy of the world and was being copied by others.
In the United Kingdom a very substantial effort has been made, as part of the national health service introduced in 1948, to overcome the shortage of doctors and dentists. In

1950, the latest date for which statistics are available, government grants were assisting some 3,178 students in medicine in the United Kingdom and 915 students in dentistry.

Practically all the universities. I can give you the names if you wish.
Another shortage that will hold up any national health plan, and which has to be overcome before you can consider it, is the shortage of nurses. This problem has been with us for many years. In fact as early as 1920 the following mention of this situation was placed on the minutes of the dominion conference on child welfare held in Ottawa on October 19 and 20 of that year:
Whereas there is a great shortage of trained and untrained nurses for the care of the sick and for public health work in the Dominion of Canada.
And whereas there is an increasing shortage of applicants to nurse training schools all over the continent-[DOT]
Various attempts have been made to measure the shortage of nurses. According to authorities, one rough guide is that there should be in hospitals one trained nurse, including the superintendent and supervisors, for every two patients. Using this guide for 1950, the latest year for which statistics are available, we find that there was an average of 53,300 patients in Canadian hospitals every day in that year. Thus, according to the rule, there should have been approximately 26,600 trained nurses, but actually there were only 14,900. In other words there was a shortage of 11,700 graduate nurses in our hospitals. But this is not the only place where the shortage of nurses is felt. Another measure, according to public health standards, is that there should be one nurse for every 280 population. If this standard were applied in Canada we should have had 53,880 practising graduate nurses in 1951, whereas according to the census we had only 35,138, a shortage of 18,742.
What is being done to meet these shortages? While the government, through its health grants program, has made some attempt to overcome the hospital shortage-although as I have indicated it is an exceedingly feeble attempt and will very likely fail in its five-year objective-there has been almost no effort at all to overcome the general shortage of nurses. There is no specific grant for assisting the training of nurses generally. Some money has been made available for assisting in the training of public health nurses, but this is only a small fraction of the problem. No concerted attempt has been made by the federal government to overcome 68108-23
The Address-Mr. Jones the general shortage of nurses. Thus it is stated in one of the government's own reports:	^
It is extremely doubtful that at current rates of output of graduate nurses the present shortage of nurses will be overcome.
The government has admitted that the health grants program is not going to overcome the shortage of nurses. Referring to the professional training grant, the data prepared by the Department of National Health and Welfare for the 57th meeting of the dominion council of health stated:
However, professional training under the health grants has. for the most part, been specialized training or refresher courses for graduate nurses and has improved the quality of nursing service provided. It has not been a factor in increasing the number of undergraduate and practical nurses in training.
I think that before solutions to the problem are proposed we should examine the reasons for the nursing shortage. Again let me quote the government memorandum:
Perhaps the most basic cause of the problem in hospital nurse education is economic in character and deeply rooted. Hospitals in Canada have always faced difficulties in meeting financial needs. In the 1870's hospitals instituted schools of nursing with the view to the function of providing nursing to hospital patients as well as education for nurses. Down through the years, the economic advantages of making large scale use of student services were apparent and it became difficult to see where nursing for the student ended and education began.
The Canadian Nurses Association listed the main reasons for this high rate of student wastage as follows: (a) physical fatigue induced by the hurry and tension in overcrowded, understaffed, wards; (b) excessively long working day; (c) imposition of duties they are not sufficiently mature to assume; (d) imposition of duties which should be assigned to domestic workers.
It is clear that the education of student nurses leaves much to be desired. Economic disadvantages, coupled with the unsatisfactory working conditions referred to by the Canadian Nurses Association, are important reasons why such a large number of girls who begin training as nurses drop out before their training is completed.
Briefly, to recapitulate what I have said, I think one of the first steps the government has to take is to establish subsidies for schools or some form of assistance for training nurses to overcome the present shortage, and to train them in public health work for the inauguration of a national health plan. As far as student nurses are concerned, the C.C.F. suggests that recognized schools of nursing could be subsidized so they do not have to use students for work in the hospitals as the major means of deferring the costs of their tuition.
As I have said before, the inauguration of a health insurance plan itself will place all hospitals in a better financial position,

The Address-Mr. Prudham including hospitals which operate schools of nursing, and this will in itself be a major factor in permitting them to provide better facilities for student nurses. In addition to this, however, subsidies are necessary to permit remuneration to student nurses, as well as better conditions and training facilities.
