I want to say that the Social Credit party has no monopoly on Christianity. These people who are always so eager to label themselves as the "Christian party of Canada" are equally fond of indulging in criticism of government policy that is often distorted, misleading and altogether unfair.
I want to deal with some subjects that provide examples of the sort of thing I have mentioned. From time to time Social Credit speakers, possibly in a light-hearted manner, have claimed that Providence delayed the recent discovery of gas and oil until a good Christian party came along to develop them. I feel it should also be said that a great deal of Christian hard work and planning had been applied to the development of Alberta's natural resources long before Social Credit, was thought of. The recent oil and gas development would not have been possible but for the federal geological surveys and studies as well as the production of federal maps ever since 1873.
From that time to the present there have been, on a yearly average, eight federal geological parties operating in what is now the province of Alberta. In addition the federal government has surveyed by air some 15,000 square miles in the province. The information gathered in this way has provided a reliable basis on which exploration for mineral wealth, including oil and gas, could be carried on. Evidence of this is shown by the fact that the department of mines and minerals of Alberta ordered 5,000 copies of the 1950 federal geological map of Alberta as soon as it was off the press.
Several hundred reports and maps directly related to possible deposits of petroleum and natural gas have been compiled and published by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. These federal government publications have been of the greatest practical

The Address-Mr. Prudham use and benefit to private companies. They were the basic reason, in many cases, why many of these companies persisted in their search. The results of this research and effort are now well recognized. Oil and gas fields of first grade importance have been developed in Alberta. This development in Alberta was no accident. It was made possible only because the region was thoroughly surveyed and mapped.
The Canadian petroleum industry still looks to the federal survey for further geological work and is guided by its findings in planning exploration programs. Geological mapping has led private enterprise to productive areas in Alberta such as Pincher Creek, Jumping Pound, Sullivan creek, Brazeau and others.
In addition, the geological survey of my department has collected 1J million drill samples, representing more than 15 million feet of drilling. These samples are studied and correlated and the information is made available to the industry. Incidentally, the government of Alberta over the past year has charged the federal government in excess of $10,000 in connection with the supply of these samples.
I should like to say a few words on the [DOT]subject of coal. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), speaking on the coal board estimates last session, expressed fear that everything possible was not being done, by subvention and otherwise, to keep the coal industry of this country in a healthy state in order to meet any national emergency that might develop. As the minister responsible to parliament for the dominion coal board I should like to draw attention to the extent to which the coal industry of Canada has been assisted by federal policy.
The subvention policy has been in effect since 1923, almost 30 years. Last year the rate of subvention assistance to western mines was increased when the railways decided to raise their flat rate on the eastward movement of Canadian coal.
The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has been assisting the coal industry in a number of ways. The department maintains an office in Calgary from which field representatives work with mine operators on coal preparation problems and improvement in coal-mining methods. In co-operation with McGill university the department is also assisting with the Mordell project. This is an experiment, under Professor Mordell's direction, toward the development of a coal-fired gas turbine engine. If it is successful, the coal industry will be helped substantially. Up until the end of the present fiscal year

the federal government will have assisted this project to the extent of $200,000.
On the other hand, so far as the coal industry is concerned, in my opinion the Alberta government, though it has collected large sums in royalties, has done little to assist the industry in a practical way. Actually a total of over $6 million in royalties, fees, rentals and mineral taxes has been collected by the Social Credit government from coal mines in Alberta since it came into office. I want to make it quite clear, however, that the Alberta research council, within the scope of its limited facilities, has co-operated at all times with federal agencies. The relations between the scientists of the council and the scientists of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys have always been most cordial and mutually helpful.
During the course of this parliament, Social Credit members have referred to the Alberta tar sands. On May 1 of this year, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), in dealing with the subject, made the following observation as reported at page 1768 of Hansard:
We remember that during the war the federal government spent around $5 million by way of investments in the tar sands of Alberta. The work done by the federal government was absolutely of no use.
The development carried out by the federal government in connection with the tar sands, from away back in 1914 up to the present time, is very little, compared with what has been done by the province, and when compared with the progress the province has made since the federal government burned up that plant at Fort McMurray.
In fairness to the facts of the situation I propose to give a brief resume of the tar sands developments. These sands, located in northern Alberta, consist of heavy oil and sand particles and in that state commercial use is difficult. The first step was to find areas where the deposits were of a sufficiently high oil content to be commercially workable. After years of preliminary surface exploration by members of the mines branch, the federal government in 1942 began an intensive search for such deposits. This work, which entailed development of a special core recovery method, led to the discovery of better grade sands in the Fort McMurray district. By means of drilling, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys proved that in an area of four and a half square miles there are deposits of oil estimated at 900 million barrels. That is sufficient, they tell me, to keep a 20,000 barrel a day refinery in operation for a hundred years.
The second step was to develop an efficient method of separating the heavy oil from the sands, and a field process of transforming it into pipe-line crude. There was also the

problem of removing the sulphur content. Federal scientists and engineers joined forces with Abasand Oils Limited to obtain a process for the economic extraction of bitumen from the sands. At this company's plant, rebuilt with federal aid, tests were made of the McClave hot water process of separation. When the plant was accidentally destroyed by fire in 1945 as the result of a spark from a welder's torch, work which had been started on a cold water process was further developed in a pilot plant set up at the mines branch in Ottawa. This plant was also used to develop means for reducing heavy oil to pipe-line crude. The results of these experiments were at all times made available to the Alberta government.
I am not discounting the activities of the provincial government, but it is time the federal government received credit for its large share in these developments.
Studies are being concentrated at the present time on the removal of sulphur from the oil, which would otherwise be very corrosive and unacceptable. This was recognized as one of the crucial problems in utilizing the oil in the report prepared by S. M. Blair, the technical consultant employed by the Alberta government. During the current year the mines branch of my department has set up equipment to carry out extensive research by hydrogenation as applied to this problem. Other tests of Alberta bitumen will also be made at the Ottawa plant.
So, as you can see, the federal government has played an important role in the development of these resources for the people of Alberta and of Canada. The scientists and engineers of my department have combined their efforts with those of private industry and of the provincial government to find the best and most practical means of utilizing the oil in the tar sands. There has always been a free exchange of information between the provincial and dominion scientists.
Such projects can only be brought to a successful conclusion by joint effort on the part of the federal and provincial governments and private enterprise. This co-operation is the key to the success of this confederation of ours. The hon. member for Bow River apparently lost sight of these facts or tried to distort them.

It is either oil or coal and, as a result, the cost of electric power in rural areas in my province is very high.
Even if the farmers in some areas were willing to pay very high rates they would have very little hope of receiving service in the near future. I feel very strongly that this situation could be relieved very considerably if a uniform method of taxing public utilities could be found, regardless of the organization of the capital structure of the service which is being extended. This state of affairs, of course, also applies to the telephone systems of some of our provinces although it may not apply in others. That again creates an uneven distribution of the federal tax load on the Canadian people.
That is all I wish to say on those matters for the moment, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to make some remarks which have a bearing on another of our industries in Prince Edward Island. One of our main industries down there, apart from fisheries and agriculture, is of course the tourist industry. For a tourist industry to be successful one of the main requirements is that the area to be visited by tourists should be readily accessible, especially by road in this modem age. Therefore a frequent and high quality service for motorists to and from Prince Edward Island is a primary requirement. That being
362	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. J. A. MacLean the case, I would like to point out to the government the difficulties under which the tourist industry in my province labours due to the bottlenecks in travel to and from the island by the two ferry services which exist. There is a ferry service from Cape Tormen-tine to Borden, operated by the Canadian National Railways. It is a very good service but, at the same time, during the peak months of the summer it is inadequate. The result is that motorists must wait for a long time on each side before getting from or to the island. I would therefore suggest that the government give serious consideration to supplying a second ferry boat on that service for summer use. It would not have to be an icebreaker. It would not have to be as expensive a boat as we have there now, but it would be a boat that would relieve the peak traffic periods during the summer when tourists are going to and from Prince Edward Island.
The other main ferry service is operated by Northumberland Ferries Limited from Wood Island to Caribou, Nova Scotia. This company finds itself in a very difficult situation because at the present time it seems to be impossible for it to acquire adequate and suitable ships for service. This service is one which has been growing very rapidly in the last few years. Traffic over the route is increasing to the point where, at the present time, the company is unable to cope with it with its present facilities. A third ferry of some description is required to be made available for next summer so that congestion on the route will be somewhat relieved. That would only be a temporary measure, and I would recommend most strongly to the government that consideration be given to either providing a boat for this company, which might be run on a management basis, or creating an environment which would allow this company to build a suitable boat for its own operations so the service could be improved.
Another matter which has some bearing on our tourist industry is the advertising which is done by various departments of the government for the purpose of attracting tourists to our province. I feel that perhaps this advertising is not sufficient. Until recently I was under the impression that the advertising was adequate, but some unfortunate circumstances with respect to my province have recently been reported in a widely-read Canadian periodical. It concerns a very well known and famous citizen of Ottawa who had occasion to go to our province last summer. Due to circumstances about which I have no information it would seem that this man was very unfortunate in the accommodation which was provided for him there. The result was that while he was spending some


time in Prince Edward Island, as quoted in this periodical, he had "the worst meal he had ever eaten in Canada".
The most unfortunate thing about this is that such a state of affairs is entirely unnecessary. I myself have eaten in most of the public eating places in Queens county and so has the senior member for Queens (Mr. McLure). I must say that in most cases the food was very good and I think, Mr. Speaker, you will agree with me when I say that both the senior member for Queens and myself look reasonably well fed.

This unfortunate gentleman, who is a great man, and being a great man no doubt is a humble man, probably has tastes that are not unnecessarily extravagant. I expect that he would have demands with regard to food which were not unreasonable. Nevertheless he apparently ended up in a fifth rate hotel because, as I said, he was served the worst meal he ever ate in Canada. I think that is most unfortunate, because with a little advertising in the right places people going from Ottawa to Prince Edward Island would have a better idea where to go. There are excellent places in Prince Edward Island at which to eat. I am quite sure every hon. member will agree with me when I say that.
For instance, the Ontario motor league publishes a booklet which is called "Travel in North America", or something of that sort, and it lists at least three hotels in my riding which have a triple A rating. I understand that is the highest rating that association gives. In addition to that, if there were any doubt about the matter, there are many places in my riding which are recommended in various travel folders as good places at which to dine. For instance, in a book called "Let us Visit Canada" by Byron Steele, which was published in 1948, a couple of places are mentioned. He refers to one as having as its specialty seafood and steaks; another serves excellent chicken dinners. I believe, therefore, that with a little suitable advertising either by the Department of Transport or the Department of Resources and Development people in the rest of Canada might be educated to such an extent that they would not have such an unfortunate experience.
This man does not say where he had the misfortune to stay. I am sure he could have stayed in some very fine hotels, one of which would be the Charlottetown hotel. I feel that if that were sufficiently advertised it would attract more notable clients from this part of the country. I see that the Canadian National Railways do put out a little booklet

advertising their hotels. It is entitled "Canadian National Railways Hotels Coast to Coast." With reference to the Charlottetown hotel, it says it has 110 rooms, each with a private bath. Then the booklet goes on to say:
Georgian in architecture, this modern fireproof structure is one of the finest in the Canadian National Railways chain of hotels. Conveniently situated close to the business and shopping district of Charlottetown, it is but a half mile from the Canadian National Railways station.
The Charlottetown is celebrated for its excellent cuisine, seafood dishes being a special feature.
I hope that it was not seafood that caused this notable gentleman a bad time, because he does admit that he is unable to distinguish a live lobster from a cooked one, not knowing that a live lobster is dark green and a cooked one is bright red. I point out this experience, Mr. Speaker, merely to give the government some small idea of the importance of good advertising to the residents of Prince Edward Island, to whom the tourist industry is of great importance. I believe this especially necessary because in my constituency we not only have a very fine Canadian National Railways hotel; we also have a very fine park, and there are some excellent privately run hotels.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, for the splendid manner in which they discharged their duties.
I also wish to congratulate the Clerk of the House on the lecture he gave at the Capitol theatre last Sunday night. I am sure that everyone present found it very interesting.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to call the attention of the government to the shortage of cement in my province, especially in my constituency. It is rather strange to find that cement becomes scarcer as the weather gets more favourable for building projects. Such a situation is annoying for people who intend to build a house or erect any other kind of building. Every season we experience the same trouble with regard to that essential building material.	-
We are well aware of the present housing situation. Therefore, in order to further the erection of housing units, production of building materials must be increased and an adequate distribution assured.
In my district, when we speak of cement, we are under the general impression, rightly or wrongly, that our people are at the mercy of the Canada Cement Company who are in 68108-241
The Address-Mr. Dube a position to supply or deny this building material to whoever wishes to build a home.
Many people wonder why there is only one cement producing company in this country where the use of this material is so widespread and, especially, when there is an inexhaustible supply of the raw materials used in the manufacturing of cement.
In my humble opinion, though I have made no personal inquiry or study of the situation, I realize that our people are the innocent prey of monopolizing interests. This opinion is also shared by our farmers and our workers who are particularly affected by the scarcity of that building material. There are some who take advantage of the present shortage to speculate and exploit those who need cement. This product, which was selling for 80 or 90 cents a bag before the shortage, now fetches ridiculous prices, such as $1.50 or $2.10, and even $3.10, I am told, in certain cases. It is easy to see that cement is being sold on the black market by individuals who, foreseeing this shortage, have accumulated stocks which they are now marketing at these exorbitant prices.
I believe it is time for the government to intervene immediately to put a stop to this kind of thing, so that the people of this country may buy, for a reasonable price, this product manufactured from our own natural resources. I am convinced that private enterprise is bound to fail unless our governments manage to set fair standards. If we want to do away with communism in our midst, let us try to inspire the people with greater confidence in the social benefits of private enterprise. People do not live from slogans, but from daily bread, from a proper distribution of goods, from equal opportunities for all, not only in theory, but in practise.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to know that the governments of Quebec and New Brunswick have finally agreed to apply to the federal government for the necessary grants for the construction of a bridge across the Restigouche river, between Campbellton, New Brunswick, and Cross Point, Quebec.
The population of the city of Campbellton has asked for the construction of this bridge for so long that it will no doubt welcome this agreement between the two provinces.
I hope that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) will respond favourably to the wishes of the people of both sides who rightly deserve that the necessary grants be accorded them for the early implementation of this project.
The city of Campbellton is now important enough, and the joining of both provinces by

The Address-Mr. Dube means of this bridge will be profitable to everyone and will be of much help in the development of activities in this area. In former days roads were bad and automobiles rather scarce. Today it is another story. Most people own automobiles and travel, especially since the completion of the trans-Canada highway.
A large number of those people who visited Gaspe this year would have crossed over to visit New Brunswick, and vice versa, if only there had been a bridge between Cross Point and Campbellton. Some motorists do not like to take the ferry, both because they do not like to wait for the return of the boat thus wasting precious moments and because they are not confident of their ability to drive their car onto it. But, mainly, it is because of the loss of time. Everything moves so quickly today. A bridge is far more convenient, there is no doubt about that.
Since both provinces are equally deserving of a visit from those who want to see all of
Canada, I really believe that the government would quickly recover the moneys put into this venture, through a constant increase in the tourist trade.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I wish to contradict the statement made by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) concerning the railway employees. According to him, their wage demands are not justified.
If the hon. member for Springfield knew of all the expense railway employees incur while at work, I am sure he would not have spoken the way he did. If he only knew the responsibilities which they face, I am sure he would not introduce in this house a bill to prevent them from striking for the next two years. Should he introduce this bill, I will vote against it.
